Set content-visibility: hidden on initially hidden heavy blocks (extra rows of a large data table, switchable views) and change it to visible or auto to reveal; wrap it in @supports (content-visibility: hidden) with display: none as the default
Opponent
Missing: the guide only says it is better than display: none, without saying what concretely goes wrong with display: none when toggling (quote: "superior to display: none")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Unsupported browsers fall back via @supports to display: none to keep hiding working, losing cached rendering state on toggle
Unlock
Use content-visibility: hidden to hide heavy blocks while preserving style/layout state for near-instant toggles

Switching back and forth between views recomputes each one every time it reappears. With content-visibility: hidden, nothing is laid out or painted while hidden, and the rendered result is kept and reused on reveal.

Support content-visibility: Newly (same as above)

mwg:defer-rendering-heavy-content:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

content-visibility can take content out of the accessibility tree and find-in-page CorrectionPartialNewly Defer rendering heavy content · Hiding or disabling locks people out
Action
Use hidden="until-found" instead of content-visibility: hidden for content that must stay searchable while hidden; when using content-visibility: auto, walk through the page with the keyboard alone to confirm off-screen nodes are still reachable in order
Opponent
content-visibility: hidden removes the element and its children from the accessibility tree and find-in-page; with auto, off-screen nodes may also be missing from the accessibility tree or sequential navigation in some assistive-tech setups until focus moves inside (quote: "In certain assistive technology configurations, off-screen nodes utilizing content-visibility: auto may be excluded from the accessibility tree or sequential navigation routes until focus is forcibly moved inside them.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers without content-visibility keep content normally visible and searchable, losing only deferred rendering

Swap collapsed content to content-visibility: hidden for performance and Ctrl+F can no longer find the text inside. Off-screen auto blocks may also be unreachable in order for some screen reader users.

Support content-visibility: Newly (same as above); hidden="until-found" support is not listed in this guide (see search-hidden-content)

mwg:defer-rendering-heavy-content:5 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use scrollend instead of debouncing to guess when scrolling is over New capabilityPartialNewly Defer work until scroll ends · Guessing when something has finished
Idea · brainstormWork like 'remember reading position by chapter' or 'load the high-res version of the image you stopped on' can run once when the user really stops, instead of several times during momentum scrolling.
Action
Listen for scrollend on the scroll container or document and put content fetching, layout recalculation and analytics beacons in that callback
Opponent
Debouncing scroll with setTimeout to guess the end is unreliable and can fire while the user is still scrolling (quote: "However, these debounced functions are notoriously unreliable. They may trigger while the user’s is still scrolling.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Unsupported browsers fall back to scroll plus setTimeout custom events, still risking premature firing from timer guesses
Unlock
Listen to scrollend to trigger callbacks right when scrolling, transitions, or gestures finish without timer guesswork

A finger still slowly dragging, or momentum scrolling not yet stopped, and the 100ms debounce has already fired, starting fetches and layout mid-scroll. scrollend lets the browser decide the real end point, with no wait time to guess.

Support scrollend: Newly (2025-12-12; Chrome 114, Edge 114, Firefox 109, Safari 26.2)

mwg:defer-work-until-scroll-ends · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Keep heavy work out of scroll callbacks CorrectionPartialNewly Defer work until scroll ends · Heavy work blocks the main thread
Action
Limit scroll callbacks to lightweight live feedback and move layout-dependent updates and data fetching to scrollend
Opponent
Layout recalculation, analytics beacons and DOM updates during scrolling saturate the main thread, causing dropped frames and layout thrashing (quote: "Executing heavy tasks—such as layout recalculations, analytics data beacons tracking, or dynamic DOM updates—during scrolling can saturate the main thread, resulting in dropped frames and layout thrashing.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Fall back to debouncing to guess when scrolling ends, so heavy work may still land mid-scroll

Measuring layout and sending a beacon on every scroll event makes scrolling stutter. Moving that work to after scrolling ends keeps the scroll itself smooth.

Support scrollend: Newly (same as above)

mwg:defer-work-until-scroll-ends:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use image-set() so CSS background images also pick the smallest file by format and resolution CorrectionWinWidely Deliver optimized decorative images · Loading more than is needed
Action
In background-image, mask-image or content, use image-set() to list AVIF/WebP/JPEG at 1x and 2x, ordered from most to least optimized format
Opponent
Missing: the guide only says this improves perceived performance and the browser picks the smallest suitable image; it doesn't say where a single url() goes wrong (quote: "Delivering optimized decorative images via CSS improves perceived performance without sacrificing visual quality.")
Fallback
Not needed — image-set() is already Widely available (a preceding single image URL guards very old browsers)

Decorative CSS images used to allow only one URL, serving neither high-DPI screens nor new formats. image-set() gives CSS images a srcset-like choice. The guide doesn't describe the concrete cost of a single URL.

Support image-set(): Widely (2023-09-18; Chrome 113, Edge 113, Firefox 89, Safari 17)

mwg:deliver-optimized-decorative-images · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't leave a likely LCP image only inside CSS image-set() CorrectionWinWidely Deliver optimized decorative images · Loading priority is misplaced
Action
Use an HTML <img> or <picture> for LCP candidates such as hero banners, or additionally preload them with <link rel=preload> and a media attribute
Opponent
Images referenced via CSS image-set() are invisible to the preload scanner, delaying their load and hurting LCP (quote: "images referenced in CSS via image-set() are not discoverable by the browser's preload scanner. This can significantly delay image loading and harm LCP.")
Fallback
Not needed — image-set() and <img> alternatives are all Widely available; no fallback needed

With the hero image as a CSS background, the browser only learns it needs it after the stylesheet downloads and applies, pushing LCP back. Moving it into HTML or a preload starts the download at the earliest point.

Support image-set(): Widely (same as above); no support data listed for <img>, <picture> or <link rel=preload>

mwg:deliver-optimized-decorative-images:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use fetch() priority: 'low' so analytics and prefetches give way to data the user is waiting for New capabilityPartialNewly Deprioritize background fetches · Loading priority is misplaced
Idea · brainstormPrefetch the next chapter, next page or thumbnails freely in the background without fear of slowing the user's current search or submit; 'guess the next step' interfaces like readers and photo albums get cheaper.
Action
Add priority: 'low' to the fetch() options for analytics, logging, background sync and prefetches of data that might be needed later; leave it off for requests critical to the experience
Opponent
Simultaneous requests compete for the same bandwidth, slowing the user-initiated critical ones (quote: "When a page performs multiple simultaneous network requests, they often compete for the same bandwidth.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Unsupported browsers ignore the option and use default priority, still sending requests without yielding to critical data
Unlock
Add priority: 'low' to background fetch() calls so non-critical requests yield bandwidth to data the user is waiting on

The user clicks, and the data the screen needs shares the line with analytics events and background sync sent at the same time. Lowering background requests lets the browser give bandwidth to the one the user is waiting on.

Support Fetch priority: Newly (2024-10-29; Chrome 103, Edge 103, Firefox 132, Safari 17.2)

mwg:deprioritize-background-fetches · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use visibility-state performance entries to tell whether the page loaded in a background tab New capabilityStalemateLimited Detect initial visibility state · Performance measurement is skewed or blind
Idea · brainstormA self-hosted RUM can tag background-opened visits automatically and report them separately, so median load times aren't inflated by people who middle-click links into new tabs. Chromium only for now.
Action
Read performance.getEntriesByType('visibility-state'); if the first entry is hidden the page loaded in the background, and the first hidden entry's startTime is when it went to the background; filter such pages out of performance analytics
Opponent
Reading document.visibilityState when the script runs is racy: a page opened in the background and foregrounded before the script finished reads visible and is misjudged as a foreground load (quote: "When your script finally runs, document.visibilityState will synchronously read as 'visible', and you will incorrectly assume the page was loaded in the foreground, completely missing its initial hidden state.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Firefox and Safari fall back to document.visibilityState, keeping startup race gaps and lower timing accuracy
Unlock
Query visibility-state performance entries for full foreground/background history so async scripts never miss background loads

Pages opened in background tabs render late and stretch metrics like FCP, skewing the stats. Async analytics scripts often run after the user has switched back, so checking only the current state misses it. Only Chromium gets the right answer.

Support Page visibility state performance entries: Limited (Chrome 115, Edge 115; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:detect-initial-visibility-state · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use contentvisibilityautostatechange to pause animations and polling while a component isn't rendered New capabilityPartialNewly Efficient background processing · Work spent on what nobody can see
Idea · brainstormPut many live canvases on one page (several stock charts, physics simulations, WebGL previews) with only the ones near the viewport running and the rest paused automatically, so the laptop fan stays quiet.
Action
Give heavy components content-visibility: auto and contain-intrinsic-size, and listen for contentvisibilityautostatechange: when event.skipped is true stop canvas animation, WebGL rendering and high-frequency WebSocket polling, otherwise resume
Opponent
Missing: the guide only says to pause heavy work when the component isn't rendered to save system resources and battery, without saying what concretely happens if it keeps running (quote: "Pause heavy background tasks when a component is not being rendered by the browser to conserve system resources and battery life.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Unsupported browsers fall back to IntersectionObserver with rootMargin to pause work nearby, losing exact rendering-lifecycle sync
Unlock
Listen to contentvisibilityautostatechange tied directly to rendering so skipped components pause heavy work automatically

Simulations, charts and live data panels scrolled off-screen keep computing every frame. Tied to this event, they stop when the browser decides not to render them and restart when it prepares to. Unlike IntersectionObserver, it maps to render timing rather than geometric visibility.

Support content-visibility: Newly (2025-09-15; Chrome 108, Edge 108, Firefox 130, Safari 26); the guide lists contentvisibilityautostatechange under the same status

mwg:efficient-background-processing · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

contentvisibilityautostatechange doesn't bubble in some implementations; delegate with capture CorrectionPartialNewly Efficient background processing · Non-bubbling events never arrive
Action
Attach the listener directly to the element with content-visibility: auto, or add { capture: true } when delegating from a parent
Opponent
The event doesn't bubble in some browser implementations, so ordinary listeners on a parent never receive it (quote: "The contentvisibilityautostatechange event does not bubble in some browser implementations.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers without this event fall back to IntersectionObserver for viewport entry/exit, avoiding bubbling pitfalls

Delegating on document out of habit means that in some browsers the event never travels up, the pause logic never runs, and nothing reports an error.

Support content-visibility: Newly (same as above)

mwg:efficient-background-processing:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Cache inactive SPA views with content-visibility: hidden so switching back needs no recomputation New capabilityPartialNewly Faster SPA view transitions via state caching · Work spent on what nobody can see
Idea · brainstormTools with three to five tabs (edit / preview / settings, or several dashboard pages) can switch with zero wait while keeping scroll position and expanded state, without a framework keep-alive mechanism.
Action
Add content-visibility: hidden (optionally with position: absolute to take no space) to inactive SPA views and remove it on switch; fall back to display: none via @supports not (content-visibility: hidden)
Opponent
Destroying the old view or hiding it with display: none both force the browser to rebuild or recompute full layout and paint when the user returns (quote: "Both approaches require the browser to recreate or recalculate the full layout and paint when the user returns to that view.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Fall back to display:none, so switching back to a view still requires recomputing layout and paint
Unlock
Use content-visibility: hidden to hide inactive SPA views while caching layout state for near-instant view switches

Switching back and forth between tabs lays out each one from scratch every time. Hiding while keeping the cache spends almost no CPU on unseen views and reuses them on return. The cost is memory; see the next line.

Support content-visibility: Newly (2025-09-15; Chrome 108, Edge 108, Firefox 130, Safari 26)

mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Caching every view exhausts memory; dynamic routes need an eviction strategy CorrectionPartialNewly Faster SPA view transitions via state caching · Over-applied optimizations backfire
Action
Cache every view only when there are few, predictable views; apps generating many reports or routes implement an eviction strategy such as LRU and destroy old views at a memory threshold
Opponent
Unconditionally caching every view eventually bloats memory badly and may crash the browser on low-end devices (quote: "Doing so will eventually cause severe memory bloat and may crash the browser on low-end devices.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers falling back to display: none still need route-based eviction of old views to prevent DOM bloat

content-visibility: hidden keeps all DOM, listeners and state, so each report opened adds another copy. With unbounded routes, a long session eventually blows up the tab.

Support content-visibility: Newly (same as above)

mwg:faster-spa-view-transitions:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use blocking="render" so experiment scripts finish before first paint, replacing page-hiding anti-flicker snippets New capabilityStalemateLimited Flicker-free client-side A/B testing · Content takes shape only after JS runs
Idea · brainstormTheme, font-size and locale preferences stored in localStorage can be applied by a tiny render-blocking module before first paint, with no flash of default styles. Not supported in Firefox.
Action
Put the experiment script in <head> with async (external) or type="module" (inline) plus blocking="render"; add blocking="render" to dynamically inserted variant stylesheets too; switch variants via a data attribute on <html>
Opponent
The script changes the DOM after the page starts building, so users see the original then a flash to the variant; traditional anti-flicker snippets hide the whole page with opacity: 0 until the script runs or about 4 seconds pass, sacrificing progressive rendering and allowing clicks on invisible content (quote: "This approach sacrifices progressive rendering, allows accidental clicks on invisible content, and introduces unnecessary paint cycles.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Firefox falls back to an opacity: 0 anti-flicker snippet, sacrificing progressive rendering and risking clicks on hidden UI
Unlock
Use blocking="render" to finish experiment scripts before first paint without blocking HTML parsing or needing anti-flicker snippets

A/B tools have long had to pick a harm: don't block and it flickers, block and the page is blank for seconds and can be misclicked. blocking="render" gives scripts the same render-blocking behavior as stylesheets, delaying paint but not parsing. Firefox still needs the old snippet.

Support blocking="render": Limited (Chrome 105, Edge 105, Safari 18.2; not Firefox)

mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

If a render-blocking script is slow or its CDN goes down, the page never paints CorrectionPartialLimited Flicker-free client-side A/B testing · Over-applied optimizations backfire
Action
Keep only a small stub that applies the variant render-blocking (for example under 100ms execution), load tracking and analytics separately with async/defer; don't put blocking="render" on non-visual scripts; consider server-side splitting for performance-critical pages
Opponent
Rendering waits until the script executes, so a large or slow script directly delays first paint; a third-party CDN outage could block rendering entirely, with no developer-controlled timeout (quote: "If the experiment SDK is hosted on a third-party CDN, a CDN outage could block rendering entirely.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Firefox ignores the attribute and falls back to timeout-bounded anti-flicker or server-side bucketing without hanging paint

Put blocking="render" on the whole experiment SDK and the flicker is gone, but every visit waits for it to download first; when the SDK host has an outage, the whole site is blank until the browser's own timeout.

Support blocking="render": Limited (same as above)

mwg:flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Replace tracking pixels in unload with fetchLater(), letting the browser send whole-visit data when the user leaves New capabilityPartialLimited Reliably measure full-session analytics and telemetry · Background sends are unreliable or excessive
Idea · brainstormA long-read page can keep updating 'read up to paragraph N, stayed this long', and the final state still arrives when the tab closes, without losing bfcache. Native in Chromium, polyfilled elsewhere.
Action
Call fetchLater() as soon as data exists; when state changes, cancel the previous one with AbortController and reschedule with the full latest snapshot; the browser sends the last scheduled payload when the user leaves or closes the tab; where unsupported, use the guide's polyfill (built on fetch keepalive or sendBeacon())
Opponent
The old trick of creating an <img> pixel in an unload listener is very unreliable (especially on mobile) and makes pages ineligible for bfcache (quote: "Older technique like creating an <img> pixel in an unload event listener are notoriously unreliably (especially on mobile) and can negatively impact performance (by making pages ineligible for bfcache).")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Firefox and Safari fall back to visibilitychange with keepalive/sendBeacon, still delivering beacons without breaking bfcache
Unlock
Update visit snapshots continuously via fetchLater() so the browser reliably sends them on page exit without breaking bfcache

Session length, whole-visit CWV and error logs are only known at the very end, and the old way forced a send on unload, which often never went out on phones and also hurt back/forward caching. fetchLater() lets the page keep updating 'what to send when leaving' and leaves the timing to the browser.

Support fetchLater: Limited (Chrome 135, Edge 135; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:full-session-analytics · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

fetchLater() has a roughly 64KB per-origin quota; keep payloads small and wrap calls in try/catch CorrectionPartialLimited Reliably measure full-session analytics and telemetry · Wrong arguments or formats throw
Action
Keep the payload minimal and wrap fetchLater() calls in try/catch to handle quota errors; don't use a ReadableStream as the body
Opponent
fetchLater() throws when the quota is exceeded, and a ReadableStream body also errors (quote: "DO NOT use a ReadableStream object for the request body, as that will error.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Falling back to visibilitychange with keepalive/sendBeacon still supports smaller payloads and error handling

A beacon rescheduled every 10 seconds carries the whole data set, which keeps growing until one call exceeds the quota and throws at the fetchLater() call. The guide asks you to shrink the payload up front and catch the error yourself.

Support fetchLater: Limited (same as above)

mwg:full-session-analytics:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use Long Animation Frames to find the scripts costing the most time on real users' devices New capabilityPartialLimited Identify heavy-running JavaScript · Performance measurement is skewed or blind
Idea · brainstormBuild a 'third-party script bill' panel: how much main-thread time each external script consumes on real users' devices, to decide whether to replace a chat widget or ad SDK. Data comes from Chromium users only.
Action
Observe long-animation-frame with PerformanceObserver (buffered: true), accumulate each entry's scripts, group by sourceURL, sum duration and rank the heaviest scripts (including third-party chat, video and analytics), then send them to an analytics service
Opponent
Lab data reproduces only a small subset of real usage and differs a lot from field data, making root causes of poor performance, especially slow interactions, hard to find; the JS Self-Profiling API has higher runtime overhead (quote: "field data is often very different to lab data, which only replicates a small subset of real user scenarios.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Firefox and Safari safely ignore this API, while most performance wins still show up in Chromium field telemetry
Unlock
Use the lightweight Long Animation Frames API in real-user sessions to pinpoint heavy scripts delaying frames

The page stutters for users but runs smoothly on the dev machine, and profiling catches nothing. LoAF makes every frame over 50ms report which scripts ran and for how long, so you can tell in production which third party is dragging.

Support Long animation frames performance entries: Limited (Chrome 123, Edge 123; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:identify-heavy-scripts · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use Event Timing to split INP into three parts and find which part is slow first New capabilityPartialNewly Identify causes of poor INP · Performance measurement is skewed or blind
Idea · brainstormAll four major browsers can report which button was slow and in which phase, so you can build a list of slow interactions ranked by target that points straight to the component to fix.
Action
Use onINP() from web-vitals/attribution to get the slowest interaction's inputDelay, processingDuration, presentationDelay and target, and send them back to analytics
Opponent
Interaction slowness depends on user actions, device and network, and lab data reproduces only a small subset of real cases, making it hard to diagnose; without splitting, it's easy to jump straight to the interaction handler (quote: "Lab data only replicates a small subset of real user scenarios so measuring the causes of slow INP in the field is essential.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Older browsers without Event Timing measure neither INP nor its three phase breakdowns at all
Unlock
Use Event Timing to split INP into input delay, processing duration, and presentation delay to find the real bottleneck phase in the field

INP is bad, so the first instinct is to optimize the button's click handler, when the real culprit is another script already running before the click, or the repaint afterward. The three-way split points the direction before digging in.

Support Event timing performance entries: Newly (2025-12-12; Chrome 76, Edge 79, Firefox 89, Safari 26.2)

mwg:identify-inp-causes · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use LoAF to separate style recalculation from layout time instead of heavy JS Self-Profiling New capabilityStalemateLimited Identify causes of poor INP · Performance measurement is skewed or blind
Idea · brainstormProduction slow-interaction reports can be labeled 'style recalculation' or 'forced layout' with the responsible script and function position attached, so whoever fixes it doesn't have to reproduce it locally first. Data from Chromium only.
Action
Read forcedStyleDuration/forcedLayoutDuration (forced synchronous work inside scripts) and styleDuration/layoutDuration (frame rendering phase) from LoAF and report them separately; where the split fields are missing, fall back to the combined forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration and totalStyleAndLayoutDuration
Opponent
A full trace with the JS Self-Profiling API is heavyweight and can itself cause performance problems (quote: "A full performance trace using the JS Self-Profiling API is a heavyweight solution that is liable to cause performance problems.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Falling back to combined fields or Firefox/Safari ignoring LoAF cannot separate style recalculation from layout time
Unlock
Use lightweight LoAF telemetry in the field to separate style recalculation and layout time without heavy profiler traces

Knowing that 'processing took long' isn't enough: style and layout are different diseases. Telling them apart used to require a full profile, but running a profiler in production slows the page itself. LoAF reports the two separately.

Support Long animation frames performance entries: Limited (Chrome 123, Edge 123; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:identify-inp-causes:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use Speculation Rules to prefetch or prerender the next page before the user clicks New capabilityStalemateLimited Improve next page load performance · Loading priority is misplaced
Idea · brainstormThe 'next step' of an online course, documentation or multi-step form can be prerendered so the page is already there on click, giving a static site instant navigation without becoming an SPA. Chromium only for now.
Action
Write prefetch/prerender rules in <script type="speculationrules">, preferring where document rules that pick links with href_matches/selector_matches, with eagerness (immediate/eager/moderate/conservative), optionally adding a tag the server can read from Sec-Speculation-Tags
Opponent
Missing: the guide only says starting to load the next page before the user visits is one of the most effective ways to improve load performance, without saying what concretely goes wrong otherwise (quote: "One of the most effective ways to improve page load performance for users navigating a site is to initiate loading the next page they're about to visit *before* they visit it.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Firefox and Safari ignore the rules and load normally on click, losing prefetch and prerender speedups
Unlock
Declare rules in <script type="speculationrules"> so the browser prefetches or prerenders the next page before the user clicks

Rules let the browser fetch or render the next page ahead of time, when the user hovers a link or even right on arrival, and you can prefetch eagerly then prerender on stronger signals with moderate eagerness. It's pure progressive enhancement: unsupported browsers gain nothing.

Support Speculation rules: Limited (Chrome 109, Edge 109; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't speculate state-changing URLs, and beware stale content on dynamic pages CorrectionPartialLimited Improve next page load performance · Actions get triggered by accident
Action
In document rules, use not to exclude URLs like /logout and add-to-cart, admin paths, and links marked .do-not-prerender or rel~=nofollow; use prerender and high eagerness cautiously on frequently changing dynamic pages
Opponent
Speculation can hit URLs that trigger state changes, and prefetched content on dynamic pages may be stale (quote: "DO NOT speculate URLs that likely trigger state changes, like /logout or /add-to-cart, and explicitly exclude them from your speculation rules if they are likely to be included in document rules.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Firefox and Safari ignore prerender rules, so no state-changing side effects can fire before click

A single href_matches: "/*" rule pulls in every same-origin link on the page, logout and add-to-cart included, so those URLs may be requested even though the user never clicked. An exclusion list is a required companion to a broad rule.

Support Speculation rules: Limited (same as above)

mwg:improve-next-page-load-performance:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use interaction-contentful-paint and soft-navigation to measure content that appears asynchronously after an interaction New capabilityStalemateLimited Measure interaction and soft-navigation paint timing · Performance measurement is skewed or blind
Idea · brainstormAn SPA can rank LCP per route, or measure the real wait from 'press Search' to results appearing, to find the slowest navigations and API responses. Chromium only for now.
Action
Observe interaction-contentful-paint and soft-navigation with PerformanceObserver (buffered: true) to attribute content painted after fetch and SPA route LCPs back to the interaction that caused them; or use web-vitals v6 with { reportSoftNavs: true }
Opponent
LCP stops after the first interaction; INP only measures to the next frame, missing content rendered after fetch() and SPA route changes; watching URLs alone over-reports changes that aren't route changes (quote: "Just monitoring URL updates can over report URL changes that are not linked to route changes (for example, anchor link changes, multiple "redirects" for a single route change).")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Firefox and Safari retain only traditional hard-navigation metrics and cannot measure post-interaction paint or soft-nav LCP
Unlock
Use interaction-contentful-paint and soft-navigation to measure async interaction paints and SPA navigation LCP

The user presses Search, the button changes color immediately (INP looks great), and results appear three seconds later. SPA page changes have no LCP at all. The new entries trace causality across fetch, await and setTimeout, measuring from the press to the content actually appearing. Chromium only for now.

Support Interaction contentful paint performance entries: Limited (Chrome 151, Edge 151; not Firefox or Safari); Soft navigation performance entries: same

mwg:interaction-paint-timing · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Match soft-navigation paints by interactionId and report duration CorrectionStalemateLimited Measure interaction and soft-navigation paint timing · Performance measurement is skewed or blind
Action
On each soft-navigation entry, seed LCP with getLargestInteractionContentfulPaint(); match later interaction-contentful-paint entries by interactionId, not navigationId; report entry.duration, not presentationTime directly
Opponent
In apps that render before calling history.pushState(), early paint entries carry the previous navigationId, so matching by it misses them; all timestamps are measured from the original hard-navigation origin, not the soft navigation start (quote: "If the application painted content *before* updating the URL (for example, rendering a view and then calling history.pushState()), those early interaction-contentful-paint entries were emitted before the soft-navigation entry and still carry the *previous* navigationId.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Without support there are no soft navigation entries to match, so the main measurement cannot be done

The intuition is 'same navigationId, same page', but frameworks often paint first and update the URL later, so the most important paint ends up filed under the previous page. Reporting presentationTime directly gives a number measured from when the whole app opened.

Support Same as above (Limited, Chrome/Edge 151 only)

mwg:interaction-paint-timing:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Long-lived SPAs can't rely on getEntriesByType('soft-navigation') CorrectionStalemateLimited Measure interaction and soft-navigation paint timing · Performance measurement is skewed or blind
Action
Receive soft-navigation entries continuously with PerformanceObserver instead of querying performance.getEntriesByType('soft-navigation') afterward
Opponent
The browser buffer keeps only the first 50 soft navigation entries (quote: "DO NOT rely on performance.getEntriesByType('soft-navigation') to monitor long-lived single-page applications, as the browser's buffer is limited to the first 50 soft navigation entries.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Without support, soft navigations cannot be observed continuously, so the main measurement cannot be done

Admin panels and mail clients stay open all day and quickly pass 50 navigations. Querying the timeline afterward silently drops everything after that, with no error.

Support Same as above (Limited, Chrome/Edge 151 only)

mwg:interaction-paint-timing:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use content-visibility: auto containment to keep one column's changes inside that column CorrectionPartialNewly Optimizing interactions in complex layouts · Heavy work blocks the main thread
Action
Add content-visibility: auto and contain-intrinsic-size to self-contained layout units like Kanban columns or data-grid regions; where unsupported, fall back to contain: layout style paint via @supports not
Opponent
In complex layouts, changing one item (dragging a card, editing a cell) triggers chained style and layout calculations that reflow the whole page, causing dropped frames and high INP (quote: "performing a minor change to a single item—such as dragging a card or editing a cell—can trigger a chain reaction of style and layout calculations that forces the browser to reflow the entire page.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Unsupported browsers fall back via @supports to contain: layout style paint, still isolating full-page reflows

Dragging a card from one column to another reflows the whole board and the drag stutters. With each column as a containment boundary, the browser knows changes inside can't affect the outside and reflows only that column.

Support content-visibility: Newly (2025-09-15; Chrome 108, Edge 108, Firefox 130, Safari 26)

mwg:interactions-in-complex-layouts · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use loading="lazy" on <video>/<audio> to defer poster and metadata requests until near the viewport New capabilityPartialLimited Lazy load video and audio · Loading more than is needed
Idea · brainstormCourse catalogs, full podcast episode lists and product demo walls packed with media can lazy-load with plain HTML, no hand-written IntersectionObserver swapping data-src, and the first screen isn't held back by dozens of posters. Chromium only for now.
Action
Add loading="lazy" to below-the-fold <video> and <audio>, paired with preload="none" (user presses play) or preload="metadata" (duration and first frame fill in once in view); autoplay also waits until near the viewport to download and play
Opponent
Even with preload="metadata" or preload="none", the browser fetches the poster immediately, and preload="metadata" still issues range requests for every player on the page (quote: "Even when preload="metadata" or preload="none" is set on a <video>, the browser eagerly fetches its poster image immediately, and preload="metadata" still initiates range requests for media headers across every player on the page.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Falling back to IntersectionObserver with data-* attributes still defers posters and media, losing only pure-HTML simplicity
Unlock
Add loading="lazy" to <video> and <audio> to defer posters, preload, and autoplay until scrolled near without JS

A tutorial page with twenty videos, all preload="none", still fetches twenty posters on load. loading="lazy" lets media elements wait until scrolled near, like images. Chromium only for now.

Support Lazy-loading media: Limited (Chrome 150, Edge 150; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Lazy video needs width and height, lazy audio needs controls, or they never load CorrectionPartialLimited Lazy load video and audio · Hidden preconditions of new features
Action
Always give <video loading="lazy"> integer width and height; always add controls to <audio loading="lazy">
Opponent
Audio without controls has no visible box, can't intersect the viewport and never loads or autoplays; video without dimensions defaults to 300×150 and may never intersect and load, or cause layout shift when it loads (quote: "an <audio loading="lazy"> element without controls cannot visibly intersect the viewport and will never load or autoplay.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Firefox and Safari ignore loading="lazy", while explicit dimensions and controls still prevent layout shifts and show controls

Background music as an audio element without controls plus lazy, or a video sized only through CSS, and the lazy-load check never succeeds, so the media quietly never shows up.

Support Lazy-loading media: Limited (same as above)

mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

The window load event doesn't wait for lazy media CorrectionPartialLimited Lazy load video and audio · Wrong lifecycle assumptions
Action
Don't use the window load event to detect when lazy <video>/<audio> has loaded
Opponent
The load event considers only eager media; lazy media doesn't count even when it starts inside the viewport (quote: "The load event fires based only on eager-loaded media, even if a loading="lazy" media element is initially inside the visual viewport.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Firefox and Safari ignore loading="lazy" and load eagerly as normal without breaking scripts that avoid waiting on deferred media

Code that waited for load before initializing a player or measuring layout gets the timing wrong once lazy is added, because the media may not have started fetching when load fires.

Support Lazy-loading media: Limited (same as above)

mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't put loading="lazy" on above-the-fold or LCP video CorrectionPartialLimited Lazy load video and audio · Loading priority is misplaced
Action
Omit the loading attribute on the hero video (it defaults to eager) and add loading="lazy" only to media below the fold
Opponent
Adding loading="lazy" to above-the-fold or LCP video delays fetching both the poster and video data (quote: "DO NOT apply loading="lazy" to above-the-fold or Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) <video> elements, as it delays fetching both the poster image and video data.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Omitting loading="lazy" on above-the-fold media keeps it loading eagerly across all browsers without hurting LCP

Adding lazy to every <video> at once means even the hero video, the first thing seen, waits for the browser's distance check before fetching its poster, slowing LCP.

Support Lazy-loading media: Limited (same as above)

mwg:lazy-load-video-and-audio:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use fetchpriority to tell the browser which image is the LCP and which hidden ones can wait New capabilityPartialNewly Optimize image priority · Loading priority is misplaced
Idea · brainstormA homepage whose first screen holds a carousel, menu images and avatars can order downloads 'main image first, the rest later' with HTML attributes alone, without cutting the carousel to one image for LCP's sake.
Action
Add fetchpriority="high" to the LCP candidate (usually the top hero image); add fetchpriority="low" to images technically above the fold but not initially visible (hidden carousel slides, mega-menu images)
Opponent
Browsers assign image priorities by heuristics, and the defaults may not match the page's LCP (quote: "Browsers use heuristics to assign loading priorities to images, but these defaults may not always align with your page's Largest Contentful Paint (LCP).")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Unsupported browsers ignore the attribute and use default heuristics, losing manual priority hints
Unlock
Use fetchpriority to prioritize LCP hero images and deprioritize hidden above-the-fold images to cut bandwidth contention

To the browser, the hero image, the five other carousel slides and the promo image in a menu look about equally important and queue together. Marking the one that matters and the ones merely hidden gives bandwidth to the image actually seen first.

Support Fetch priority: Newly (2024-10-29; Chrome 103, Edge 103, Firefox 132, Safari 17.2)

mwg:optimize-image-priority · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

fetchpriority on the wrong images: too many highs, low on lazy below-the-fold images CorrectionPartialNewly Optimize image priority · Loading priority is misplaced
Action
Give fetchpriority="high" to at most 1–2 critical images and never combine it with loading="lazy"; ordinary below-the-fold images get only loading="lazy", not fetchpriority="low"; never lazy-load the LCP image
Opponent
Too many high images contend for the network and dilute the boost; lazy below-the-fold images also marked low don't load at normal priority when scrolled to (quote: "Only use fetchpriority="high" on at most 1-2 critical images to avoid network contention and diluting the priority boost.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers without fetchpriority safely ignore it while regular images still use loading="lazy"

The instinct with a new attribute is to mark every important image high and everything else low; the highs cancel each other out and images below the fold crawl in when scrolled to. Priority is relative and only means something when few images are boosted.

Support Fetch priority: Newly (same as above)

mwg:optimize-image-priority:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use <link rel=preload fetchpriority="high"> so preloaded key images stop queuing at low priority New capabilityPartialNewly Optimize preload priority · Loading priority is misplaced
Idea · brainstormLanding pages whose first screen is a video or a CSS background image can get the poster or background into the first slot just like an <img> hero, without changing the design for LCP's sake.
Action
Use <link rel="preload" as="image" fetchpriority="high"> for images the browser can't discover early but the page needs (video posters, hero images in CSS backgrounds); use fetchpriority="low" for preloads of secondary fonts or background video
Opponent
Preloads inherit the resource type's default priority, which for images is low (quote: "However, preloads inherit the default priority for the resource type and for images in particular this is low.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Unsupported browsers ignore fetchpriority, leaving preloaded images at that resource type's default low priority
Unlock
Add fetchpriority to <link rel=preload> to override default resource priority so critical images download earlier

You finally use preload to tell the browser about the hero background early, and it gets queued at low priority, losing to everything else. Adding fetchpriority="high" makes early discovery mean early download.

Support Fetch priority: Newly (2024-10-29; Chrome 103, Edge 103, Firefox 132, Safari 17.2)

mwg:optimize-preload-priority · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Too many preloads compete for bandwidth, and a wrong as wastes the preload CorrectionPartialNewly Optimize preload priority · Loading priority is misplaced
Action
Preload at most about 2 images and 2–3 essential fonts per page, give fetchpriority="high" to at most 1–2; write as and type correctly; prefer a static HTML <img> over preloading key images
Opponent
Too many preloads compete for bandwidth, and with an incorrect as the preload isn't used (quote: "DO: Limit the total number of preloads on a page to at most 2 images and 2-3 essential fonts to prevent bandwidth contention.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When fetchpriority is unsupported, capping preload count and using accurate as attributes still prevents wasted fetches

Preloading everything is the same as preloading nothing: it all fights for bandwidth. With a wrong as, what the preload fetched can't be used by the page, so it was fetched for nothing.

Support Fetch priority: Newly (same as above)

mwg:optimize-preload-priority:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use <script fetchpriority> so critical scripts download first and non-essential ones step aside New capabilityPartialNewly Optimize script priority · Loading priority is misplaced
Idea · brainstormA page loaded with chat widgets, analytics, and A/B-testing scripts can get its interactive app script in first using only HTML attributes, without rewriting third-party scripts into deferred manual injection.
Action
Add fetchpriority="high" to critical async/defer scripts that matter for INP; add fetchpriority="low" to analytics, ads, below-the-fold widgets, and parser-blocking scripts at the end of the body
Opponent
Browsers assign script priority by position and async/defer, so late-body scripts compete for bandwidth with more critical resources (quote: "Use fetchpriority="low" on parser-blocking scripts at the end of the body to prevent them from contending for bandwidth with more critical resources.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Unsupported browsers ignore fetchpriority and fall back to default script scheduling without manual prioritization
Unlock
Use <script fetchpriority> to explicitly prioritize critical scripts or deprioritize non-essential ones

Analytics and the main app script are both async, so the browser can't tell which matters and fetches them together. Marking high/low lets the developer decide the order; it's progressive enhancement, so older browsers just keep their default.

Support Fetch priority: Newly (2024-10-29; Chrome 103, Edge 103, Firefox 132, Safari 17.2)

mwg:optimize-script-priority · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Give fetchpriority="high" to too many scripts and they all compete again CorrectionPartialNewly Optimize script priority · Loading priority is misplaced
Action
Use fetchpriority="high" on at most 1–2 critical scripts; don't mark every <script>, only change the default when it's known to be sub-optimal
Opponent
Marking too many scripts high causes network contention and dilutes the boost (quote: "Only use fetchpriority="high" on at most 1-2 critical scripts to avoid network contention and diluting the priority boost.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Unsupported browsers safely ignore fetchpriority, and keeping annotations minimal avoids disrupting default loading

Marking every script high is the same as marking none; only with a limit does priority mean anything.

Support Fetch priority: Newly (same as above)

mwg:optimize-script-priority:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use <?start>/<?marker> and <template for> to send the shell first and patch late content in the same stream New capabilityPartialLimited Out-of-order HTML streaming · Loading priority is misplaced
Idea · brainstormPurely server-rendered pages (no front-end framework) can do "shell first, slow parts later": the article shows immediately while comments and related posts stream in once computed. Native support is Chromium-only.
Action
Place processing instructions <?marker name> or <?start name>…<?end> (wrapping a loading fallback) early in the document; later in the same response stream send <template for="name"> and the browser swaps it in. Stream critical above-the-fold UI first and use placeholders for expensive blocks like comments, ads, and related content
Opponent
The guide only calls this an alternative to traditional top-to-bottom linear HTML processing, without saying when linear processing goes wrong (quote: "an alternative to the traditional "top-to-bottom" linear processing of HTML")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Firefox and Safari keep slot replacement working via template-for-polyfill, losing only script-free native support
Unlock
Stream a shell first and fill slow chunks later in one stream via processing instructions and <template for> without top-down order coupling

A slow block in the middle of the document used to hold up everything after it. With placeholders filled in later in the stream, order is no longer tied to document order; native support is Chromium-only for now.

Support <template for>: Limited (Chrome 150, Edge 150; not Firefox or Safari). HTML processing instructions: same (unsupported browsers parse <?marker> etc. as comments, which the polyfill still recognizes)

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use streamHTML() to pipe a fetch response straight into the DOM instead of waiting for a full JSON payload New capabilityPartialNo browser support Out-of-order HTML streaming · Content takes shape only after JS runs
Idea · brainstormIsland-style pages whose server returns HTML fragments could stream new content into the main region piece by piece after a link click, with no JSON API or client templates. No native browser support for the streaming setters yet.
Action
Use the new HTML setter family (setHTML(), streamHTML(), streamAppendHTML(), 24 methods with Safe/Unsafe variants) and pipeTo(el.streamHTML()) a fetch response so the browser renders as chunks arrive
Opponent
The guide only says this replaces waiting for a full JSON payload and building the DOM by hand, without saying when that goes wrong (quote: "Stream large UI transitions in SPAs using streamHTML() instead of waiting for a full JSON payload and manual DOM construction.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Fall back to the html-setters polyfill, losing the native streaming setters
Unlock
Pipe fetch streams straight into the DOM with streamHTML() to paint incrementally without waiting or manual chunking

SPA navigations wait for the whole JSON and then assemble the DOM by hand. Streaming setters would let HTML render as it arrives, but today it's only an API shape propped up by a polyfill.

Support HTML setter methods: Limited (Supported by: Chrome 157, Edge 157. Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari.); HTML streaming setters (streamHTML() etc., this line's key feature): "not natively supported by any major browser yet.", so the line stays at no browser support

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Put the live region around the progress text only, not the streamed content, and don't use role="alert" CorrectionWinWidely Out-of-order HTML streaming · Over-announcing
Action
Apply live-region markup only to the container for progress text like "Loading…"; don't wrap the whole content in a live region; don't use role="alert" for progress
Opponent
Wrapping the whole content in a live region makes screen readers read out everything patched in when streaming completes; role="alert" makes NVDA say "Alert" first (quote: "Do not wrap the entire content in a live region, as this will cause screen readers to announce the full "patched" content when streaming is complete, which can overwhelm screen reader users.")
Fallback
Not needed — aria-live mechanisms are already Widely available; no separate fallback needed

Trying to tell screen-reader users the content has arrived ends up reading the entire block at once. Shrinking the live region to the progress text gives just enough notice.

Support aria-live: no support data in the guide; recorded as Widely following an existing line (mwg:language-model:3)

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't put the progress notice inside an aria-busy="true" panel CorrectionWinWidely Out-of-order HTML streaming · Announcements mistimed or unreliable

Set aria-busy="true" on the containers being updated and back to false when done; keep the live-region notification outside those panels
Opponent
With the notification inside an aria-busy="true" panel, screen readers wait until all content has loaded before announcing it (quote: "Do not nest the live region-based notification inside panels with aria-busy="true", as this will prevent screen readers announcing the live region until after all of the content has been loaded.")
Fallback
Not needed — aria-busy and aria-live are both Widely available; no separate fallback needed

A dashboard streams in several panels slowly, but the progress notice is wrapped inside a busy panel, so by the time it can be read it no longer means anything.

Support aria-busy / aria-live: no support data in the guide; recorded as Widely following existing lines

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't let focus vanish when a placeholder is replaced CorrectionWinWidely Out-of-order HTML streaming · Rebuilding the DOM loses state
Action
Preserve focus when replacing a placeholder that contains the active element; keep focus where it is during and after loading rather than moving it to new content (SPA navigation is the exception: move focus to the start of the new content when streaming completes)
Opponent
If a placeholder contains the focused element, focus is lost when it's replaced (quote: "make sure that focus is not lost if a placeholder containing the active element is replaced.")
Fallback
Not needed — Standard DOM focus management is already Widely available; no separate fallback needed

A keyboard user is sitting on a link inside a placeholder; the streamed content arrives, the whole block is swapped, and focus falls back to the top of the page. Preserve focus on replacement, or keep it somewhere that won't be swapped.

Support Uses plain DOM focus handling with no new feature; no support data in the guide, recorded as Widely (same treatment as :3 and :4)

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:5 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Reserve placeholder size up front so patched content doesn't shove the layout CorrectionWinWidely Out-of-order HTML streaming · Layout unexpectedly overflows or shifts
Action
Give placeholders stable dimensions; when the final size is unknown, use skeleton screens or CSS aspect-ratio to reserve space
Opponent
Placeholders without dimensions make the layout jump when content is patched in (quote: "Always provide stable dimensions for placeholders. If the final content size is unknown, use skeleton screens or CSS aspect-ratio to reserve space and prevent jarring shifts.")
Fallback
Not needed — Space reservation with aspect-ratio is already Widely available; no separate fallback needed

Out-of-order streaming makes content arrive late, and late content without a reserved spot pushes the whole page down while the user is reading.

Support aspect-ratio: no support data in the guide; recorded as Widely following an existing line (mwg:css-layout:2)

mwg:out-of-order-html-streaming:6 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use async/defer and inline critical CSS to stop render-blocking @import and big scripts in the head CorrectionWinN/A Performance · Loading priority is misplaced

Inline above-the-fold CSS in <head> and defer the rest; give every non-critical script async or defer (type="module" defers by default); split stylesheets with <link media>; load third-party scripts with defer near the end of the page
Opponent
@import in CSS creates sequential request chains that delay the CSSOM; large non-critical scripts in the head stop DOM construction until they're downloaded, parsed, and executed (quote: "This halts DOM construction until the script is downloaded, parsed, and executed.")
Fallback
Not needed — Support status is N/A; no separate fallback needed

One big script in the head and one @import in a stylesheet keep the page on a white screen. Inline what's critical, defer the rest, and the first paint doesn't wait for unimportant things.

Support No browser support data in the guide; recorded as N/A

mwg:performance · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Put the LCP image in the raw HTML, don't lazy-load it, and don't make JS or CSS its only source CorrectionWinN/A Performance · Loading priority is misplaced
Action
Make the LCP image appear in the raw HTML as an <img> (or <link rel="preload" as="image">) with fetchpriority="high"; never add loading="lazy" to above-the-fold images; don't use JS loaders to render the hero

Not needed — Support status is N/A; no separate fallback needed

When the biggest image is hidden in JS or marked lazy, the browser has to wait for layout or for scripts to run before it knows to fetch it. Written directly in the HTML, the scanner finds it immediately.

mwg:performance:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Priority is zero-sum: give too many resources high priority or preloads and they cancel out CorrectionWinN/A Performance · Loading priority is misplaced
Action
Reserve fetchpriority="high" for LCP images; fonts are already high priority so don't add it there; don't preload every font
Opponent
Elevating too many resources causes network contention and negates the boost; preloading all fonts starves other critical assets (quote: "Prioritization is a zero-sum mechanism. Elevating too many resources creates network contention and negates the benefit.")

Yield with scheduler.yield() so the continuation goes to the front of the queue, not the back New capabilityWinN/A Performance · Heavy work blocks the main thread

Service Worker caching needs per-type strategies, versioning, and limits CorrectionWinN/A Performance · Caching strategy misapplied

mwg:resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use scheduler.postTask() to sort work into user-blocking / user-visible / background New capabilityPartialLimited Schedule tasks by priority · Heavy work blocks the main thread
Idea · brainstormA notes or document editor can put typing response first, preview re-render in the middle, and search indexing and sync in the background, so typing doesn't stutter on a single main thread. Safari needs the polyfill.

Use priority: 'user-blocking' for input handling and critical rendering, the default user-visible for visible but non-blocking content, and background for analytics and prefetching; conditionally load scheduler-polyfill where unsupported
Opponent
The guide only says current-view work matters more than analytics or prefetching and that the browser should stay responsive to input, without saying when unprioritized work goes wrong (quote: "Completing tasks for the current view is more important than sending analytics or prefetching assets.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Safari conditionally loads scheduler-polyfill to preserve task priorities, at the cost of shipping extra JS
Unlock
Schedule work across three priority tiers with scheduler.postTask() so background work never blocks input

Analytics, prefetching, and UI updates used to sit in one queue, first come first served. With three tiers, background work runs only when things are idle; Safari needs the polyfill.

Not needed — Select menus, guest checkout, and backend data minimization are universal design practices independent of browser features

The recipient generates a non-extractable key pair with crypto.subtle.generateKey('MLKEM768-X25519', false, …), stores it in IndexedDB, and exports the public key as 'raw-public'; for each message the sender calls encapsulateKey() to get a one-time shared key and ciphertext capsule, encrypts with ChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-GCM, and sends { capsule, iv, ciphertext }
Opponent
The guide only says the hybrid KEM keeps the shared secret secure as long as either algorithm holds, without saying when classical-only key exchange goes wrong (quote: "it combines post-quantum ML-KEM (standardized in NIST FIPS 203) with classical 'X25519' so the shared secret remains secure as long as either algorithm holds.")

Not needed — crossorigin is an existing HTML attribute without browser support issues

You add an integrity check and the file doesn't load at all, because the browser can't see the content to compare.

Support Same as mwg:secure-external-subresources; recorded as Widely

mwg:secure-external-subresources:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

background-image, content, border-image-source, and @import fetch in no-cors mode by default, and the opaque response can't be hash-verified (quote: "background-image, content, border-image-source, and @import default to no-cors mode (producing an opaque response that cannot be hash-verified)")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Falling back to <link> and document policy verifies stylesheets, but CSS-loaded fonts and images remain unverified

mwg:secure-external-subresources:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't put an unverified fallback in the same @font-face src list CorrectionStalemateLimited Secure external subresources with SRI, CORS, and Referrer Policy · Defenses configured into no-ops
Action
Do progressive enhancement with **separate** src: declarations: first a plain url(), then a version with only cross-origin()/referrer-policy(), and finally the version with integrity()
Opponent
With verified and unverified URLs in one comma-separated src, a tampered font from the CDN fails the check, is treated as a load failure, and the browser falls back to the second, unverified URL (quote: "in a single src descriptor bypasses Subresource Integrity at runtime")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Fall back to plain url() fonts, so tampered content is not blocked by SRI

An extra fallback for compatibility turns into a back door: once verification fails, the browser obligingly loads the same file unverified.

Support Same as mwg:secure-external-subresources:3; recorded as Limited

mwg:secure-external-subresources:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Requests to third-party hosts leak origin or path information in the Referer header (quote: "Overrides the document referrer policy to prevent leaking any origin or path information in the Referer request header to the third-party host.")

Not needed — referrerpolicy and Referrer-Policy are already Widely available; no fallback needed

Every file loaded from a CDN also tells the CDN which page the user is reading. Turn it off per resource, and let the document-level policy catch the rest.

Support Same as mwg:secure-external-subresources; recorded as Widely

mwg:secure-external-subresources:5 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

An allowlist looks strict but really trusts every endpoint on that domain. With a nonce, what you trust is the handful of <script> tags you wrote into this very response.

Adding nonces to every <script> in already-rendered HTML with a regular expression cannot tell developer scripts from ones injected via reflected or stored HTML, so it authorizes the attacker's scripts (quote: "authorizing attacker-injected scripts under script-src 'nonce-...'.")

To ship CSP quickly, some sites scan the output and stamp every <script>. That hands CSP's core decision to a regex, and a regex can't tell friend from foe.

mwg:security:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Keep untrusted strings out of dangerous sinks and enforce it at runtime with Trusted Types CorrectionWinN/A Web security · Untrusted content parsed as HTML

Set text with textContent/innerText; insert untrusted HTML with setHTML(); build elements with document.createElement or DOMParser instead of concatenating HTML strings; add require-trusted-types-for 'script' to CSP and route necessary sink writes through a named trustedTypes.createPolicy(), never a pass-through policy

mwg:security:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Start HSTS with a short max-age and raise it gradually CorrectionWinN/A Web security · Legitimate connections blocked by security rules

Send Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload to force HTTPS; in production start with a max-age of about 300 seconds and raise it step by step to a year
Opponent
Sending a long max-age from day one means a misconfiguration makes the site unreachable in every browser that saw the header until the cache expires (quote: "A misconfigured HSTS with a long max-age can render the site permanently inaccessible until the cache expires in every browser that saw it.")

Not needed — HSTS headers and max-age are existing mechanisms without new feature support issues

Support HSTS: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use the __Host- prefix and HttpOnly on session cookies CorrectionWinN/A Web security · Sensitive data leaks

A session cookie without HttpOnly can be read by injected client-side scripts (quote: "Set HttpOnly (httpOnly: true) on session and authentication cookies so they cannot be read by injected client-side scripts")
Fallback
Not needed — Cookie attributes and prefixes are existing mechanisms without new feature support issues

Once a page has XSS, any script that can read cookies can walk off with the session. Make the cookie unreachable to scripts and a big chunk of the damage disappears.

Support Cookie attributes and prefixes: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:5 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Switch apps embedded in third-party pages to partitioned cookies New capabilityWinN/A Web security · Legitimate connections blocked by security rules
Idea · brainstormWhen third-party cookies got blocked, comment boxes, support chats, and payment widgets embedded in other sites forgot their users → now partitioned cookies keep sign-in and preferences within each site without turning the widget into a cross-site tracker. Fallback
Not needed — Partitioned is an existing cookie attribute without new feature support data in this guide
Unlock
Previously blocking third-party cookies broke embedded widget state; partitioned cookies give each embedding site its own isolated jar

Embedded widgets have long relied on third-party cookies to remember users, and browsers are closing that road. The way out the guide points to is partitioned cookies: one jar per embedding site.

Support CHIPS (Partitioned): the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:6 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Pick a frame-ancestors tier per embedding need, and drop X-Frame-Options for cross-origin partners CorrectionWinN/A Web security · Legitimate connections blocked by security rules

No framing: frame-ancestors 'none' plus X-Frame-Options: DENY; same-origin only: 'self' plus SAMEORIGIN; specific cross-origin partners: only frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted-partner.com, omitting X-Frame-Options

Not needed — frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options are existing mechanisms without new feature support issues

X-Frame-Options can only say block everything or same-origin only; ALLOW-FROM has long been unsupported. When you need to allow a specific partner, keeping XFO locks that partner out in some clients.

Support frame-ancestors, X-Frame-Options: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:7 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Idea · brainstormUsing SharedArrayBuffer used to require every third-party image, font, and video host to add CORP → now in-browser Wasm thread tools (video transcoding, local image processing) can enable isolation while still embedding outside assets. Mainly Chrome for now

Only isolate when SharedArrayBuffer is needed (e.g. WebAssembly threads); in Chromium prefer Document-Isolation-Policy: isolate-and-credentialless, which strips credentials from non-CORS cross-origin fetches instead of blocking them; use isolate-and-require-corp when blocking is wanted

The cross-browser path (COOP: same-origin plus COEP: require-corp) requires every embedded subresource to send a CORP header or the browser won't load it (quote: "Every embedded subresource (images, styles, external media) MUST serve an explicit Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header or the browser will prevent it from loading.")

Loses the main benefit — Falling back to cross-browser COOP+COEP still requires every third-party subresource to opt in with CORP headers

Turning on isolation for SharedArrayBuffer used to mean every third-party image needed its host to add a header, or it broke. The new policy loads them without cookies instead, but only in Chrome for now.

Support Document-Isolation-Policy: the guide says "supported primarily in Chrome (142+) and other vendors have not yet shown interest"; recorded as Limited

mwg:security:8 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use Fetch Metadata to reject cross-site requests before authentication CorrectionWinN/A Web security · Sensitive data leaks
Action
On the server check Sec-Fetch-Site/Sec-Fetch-Mode/Sec-Fetch-Dest, reject cross-site requests to non-navigational endpoints before any authentication or authorization check; add Vary: Sec-Fetch-Dest, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Site; drop same-site from the allowlist if any subdomain hosts user content

Rejecting only after authentication leaks timing information about whether a resource or session exists; without Vary, an intermediate CDN may serve cached responses to attackers (quote: "Reject disallowed requests *before* authentication or authorization checks, so the response does not leak timing information about whether a resource or session exists.")

Not needed — Fetch Metadata uses existing request headers without new feature support data in this guide

The cross-site request gets blocked, but if the block comes after looking up the account, an attacker can infer existence from response time alone. Reject first, then look up, and keep caches separated.

Support Fetch Metadata: the guide gives no browser support data (its example lets legacy browsers without Sec-Fetch-Site through); recorded as N/A

mwg:security:9 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Credentialed CORS must echo a specific origin, not * CorrectionWinN/A Web security · Legitimate connections blocked by security rules

Opponent
Setting Access-Control-Allow-Origin to * when Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is required makes the browser reject the response (quote: "Use wildcard * for Access-Control-Allow-Origin if Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is required — the browser will reject the response.")
Fallback
Not needed — CORS is an existing mechanism without new feature support issues

CORS is a grant, not a defense, and the usual mistake is granting too much. The wildcard-plus-cookies combo is one the browser simply refuses to read.

Support CORS: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:10 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Send a complete Clear-Site-Data on logout CorrectionWinN/A Web security · Sensitive data leaks
Action
Have the logout endpoint respond with Clear-Site-Data: "cookies", "storage", "cache", all three directives
Opponent
Omitting any one leaves active session cookies, Web Storage state, or cached authenticated pages in the browser (quote: "omitting any of these directives leaves active session cookies, Web Storage state, or cached authenticated pages behind.")
Fallback
Not needed — Clear-Site-Data is an existing response header without new feature support issues

The logout button was pressed and the server session deleted, yet the browser cache still holds the previous account page. The next person at a shared computer just presses Back.

Support Clear-Site-Data: the guide gives no browser support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:security:11 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use SRI only on immutable, versioned assets CorrectionWinN/A Web security · Legitimate connections blocked by security rules
Action
Add integrity (preferring sha384, sha512, or sha256) with crossorigin="anonymous" to third-party scripts and stylesheets, with the CDN sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin; only for pinned-version URLs
Opponent
Putting SRI on dynamic or unversioned assets means the hash stops matching on the next silent update and the script fails to run (quote: "Use SRI for dynamic or unversioned assets — silent updates will cause script execution to fail.")
Fallback
Not needed — SRI support is covered in secure-external-subresources; this overview states usage principles only

SRI exists precisely to refuse changed content, so binding it to an auto-updating file means the site breaks itself on the upstream's next release day.

mwg:security:12 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use Trusted Types so dangerous sinks only accept policy-made objects New capabilityPartialNewly Prevent DOM-based XSS attacks with Trusted Types · Untrusted content parsed as HTML
Idea · brainstormConfirming no innerHTML slipped through used to rely on code review and grep → now comment sections, Markdown previews, and CMS editors can have the browser guarantee across all four engines that any unsanitized write throws and gets reported
Action
Define sanitizing policies with trustedTypes.createPolicy() (delegating to DOMPurify or the app's escaping rules), convert to TrustedHTML/TrustedScriptURL before writing to sinks such as innerHTML, document.write(), <script src>, and Worker(); enforce with CSP require-trusted-types-for 'script' and restrict policy names with the trusted-types directive
Opponent
These DOM APIs accept raw strings by default, so a string carrying malicious script from an untrusted source gets executed (quote: "If a string contains malicious script from an untrusted source, it can be executed.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Older browsers only keep code running via a tinyfill while sinks still accept raw strings, losing browser enforcement
Unlock
Previously keeping raw strings out of innerHTML relied on grep and code review; dangerous sinks now accept only policy objects and throw on leaks

Asking everyone not to use innerHTML is one thing; guaranteeing no code path ever pushes a raw string into it is another. Trusted Types hands the latter to the browser: any stray write throws.

Support Trusted Types: Newly available (2026-02-24). Supported by: Chrome 83, Edge 83, Firefox 148, Safari 26

mwg:trusted-types · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Collect violations in Report-Only first; enforce Trusted Types only once they reach zero CorrectionPartialNewly Prevent DOM-based XSS attacks with Trusted Types · Legitimate connections blocked by security rules
Action
First confirm the framework and third-party libraries produce TrustedHTML/TrustedScript; send Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: require-trusted-types-for 'script', optionally registering a temporary default policy that logs where strings still arrive; switch to the enforcing Content-Security-Policy once reports drop to zero
Opponent
Enforcing while some sink writes aren't migrated, or while the framework or libraries don't produce Trusted Types, breaks the application (quote: "it carries a risk of site breakage if every sink write hasn't been migrated.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Rolling out Report-Only before enforcement works in supporting browsers, while unsupported ones have no enforcement anyway

Trusted Types protects by always throwing, and the same trait can take the site down the moment it's switched on. Observe, fix, and only then enforce.

Support Same as mwg:trusted-types; recorded as Newly

mwg:trusted-types:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Character escaping is not an HTML sanitizer CorrectionPartialNewly Prevent DOM-based XSS attacks with Trusted Types · Defenses configured into no-ops
Action
Use element.textContent (not a Trusted Types sink) when only plain text is needed; use a full sanitizer (DOMPurify or element.setHTML()) when accepting markup or attributes; never interpolate escapePolicy.createHTML() output into another HTML template
Opponent
Interpolating character-escaped strings into unquoted attributes or URL attributes like href leaves javascript: URLs un-neutralized by entity escaping (quote: "a URL attribute (<a href="${escaped}">, where javascript: URLs are not neutralized by entity escaping)")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers without Trusted Types lack escaping policies anyway, so using textContent or a full sanitizer stays equally safe

An escaping policy makes Trusted Types stop complaining, so it looks like the check passed. But &lt; can't save you from javascript:alert(1): it has no angle brackets to begin with.

Support Same as mwg:trusted-types; recorded as Newly

mwg:trusted-types:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Replace string prefix checks with Origin.from() plus isSameOrigin() New capabilityPartialLimited Compare and validate web origins and sites · Verifying the wrong identity
Idea · brainstormEvery postMessage receiver used to parse URLs and handle default ports itself → now embedded checkouts, sign-in popups, and cross-window widgets can hand the event straight to Origin.from() and compare in one line. Not yet in Firefox
Action
For privileged actions such as cross-window postMessage commands or deciding whether to attach credentials, convert both sides to Origin objects with Origin.from() (MessageEvent, <a>, and URL can be passed directly) and compare scheme, host, and port with isSameOrigin(); wrap calls in try/catch so invalid URLs and "null" return false

A startsWith() prefix check is bypassed by https://app.example.com.attacker.example; full URLs with paths or explicit default ports don't match under string equality (quote: "Checking url.startsWith('https://app.example.com') is bypassed by 'https://app.example.com.attacker.example'.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When Origin is unavailable, parsing via URL and comparing .origin still blocks prefix spoofing
