Previously string origin checks suffered from prefix spoofing and default ports; Origin.from() and isSameOrigin() compare parsed origin tuples safely

Prefix checks always pass in tests, because nobody tests with app.example.com.attacker.example. With structured origin objects you compare the parsed triple, not whether strings look alike.

Support Origin: Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 145, Edge 145, Safari 26.5. Unsupported in: Firefox

mwg:validate-origins · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use isSameSite() for cross-subdomain redirects and links New capabilityPartialLimited Compare and validate web origins and sites · Verifying the wrong identity
Idea · brainstormCorrect same-site checks used to mean shipping a Public Suffix List to the front end → now services spread across subdomains (billing, help center, main site) can safely allow redirects between each other without being spoofed by neighbors on the same public suffix. Not in Firefox

When validating post-login ?returnTo= targets or classifying links as internal vs. external, convert with Origin.from() and call isSameSite() for a schemeful same-site comparison

Splitting hostnames on . to decide same-site gets multi-label public suffixes like .co.uk and .github.io wrong and ignores http vs. https (quote: "Splitting hostnames on . to check same-site relationships fails on multi-label public suffixes (such as .co.uk or shared hosting domains like .github.io) and ignores scheme mismatches (http: vs. https:).")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Fall back to private domain rules or a Public Suffix List library, and compare the scheme

Previously checking same-site on the client meant bundling a public suffix list; isSameSite() uses the browser's built-in list directly

Take the last two labels of a.co.uk and b.co.uk and both are co.uk, so they look like one site. The right answer was always inside the browser; it just wasn't exposed.

Support Same as mwg:validate-origins; recorded as Limited

mwg:validate-origins:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Tell sandboxed iframes apart with Origin.from(event) New capabilityPartialLimited Compare and validate web origins and sites · Verifying the wrong identity
Idea · brainstormTelling several sandboxed iframes on one page apart used to require event.source or a separate MessageChannel → now plugin systems, user code previews, and multiple third-party widgets can each live in a sandbox while their messages still map reliably to the sender. Not in Firefox

When receiving messages from a sandboxed iframe (sandbox="allow-scripts"), extract the underlying opaque origin with Origin.from(event), pin it once at initialization from the expected iframe, then compare with isSameOrigin(); use new Origin() as a match-nothing sentinel before pinning; reject redirect targets whose origin.opaque is true

Keeps core behavior — Fall back to event.source or MessageChannel, no longer comparing against the null string
Unlock
Previously sandboxed iframe messages all showed origin "null"; opaque origins can now be pinned and compared

Locking untrusted code inside a sandboxed iframe is a good idea, but every sandbox signs its mail "null". The new API lets the browser say whether this message came from the same sandbox as the last one.

Support Same as mwg:validate-origins; recorded as Limited

mwg:validate-origins:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Both sides of the Origin API must be Origin objects, and calls need try/catch CorrectionPartialLimited Compare and validate web origins and sites · Wrong arguments or formats throw
Action
Run both sides through Origin.from() before comparing; get the current context's origin with Origin.from(self); fall back to parsing event.origin for synthetic test MessageEvents; wrap every call on runtime input in try/catch returning false
Opponent
Passing a raw string to isSameOrigin(), passing Location/Document to Origin.from(), or synthesizing events with new MessageEvent() in unit tests all throw a TypeError (quote: "passing a raw string throws a TypeError.")

The new API is stricter than strings, strict enough to throw on the wrong type. When an origin check throws, the whole message handler stops, so every call needs a fallback.

Support Same as mwg:validate-origins; recorded as Limited

mwg:validate-origins:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Confirm email ownership without sending mail, using autocomplete="email-verification-token" New capabilityStalemateLimited Verify email address ownership · Sign-in interrupts the user
Idea · brainstormVerifying an email used to mean switching to the inbox and copying a code → now sign-up, checkout, and newsletter subscription can finish verification on the same page, almost frictionless for users of participating providers like Gmail. Chrome origin trial only for now
Action
Put an autocomplete="email" field and a hidden autocomplete="email-verification-token" input carrying a server-side nonce in the same <form>; the browser checks the domain's DNS record, obtains an Email Verification Token from the email provider, binds it to the origin and nonce, and submits it; if the backend verifies it, skip the one-time code or magic link

The traditional one-time code or magic link makes users leave the page, wait for mail, and copy codes, causing drop-off and phishing risk, and tells the email provider which site the user is visiting (quote: "This forces users to leave your page, wait for email delivery, and copy codes—introducing friction, drop-off, and phishing risk, while also revealing to the email provider which relying party (RP) the user is visiting.")

Loses the main benefit — When unsupported or the email provider does not participate, fallback sends a one-time code or magic link, requiring users to leave the page
Unlock
Previously verifying email meant sending mail, waiting, and copying codes while leaking the visited site; browsers now present proof without sending mail or leaking the relying party

Go check your inbox and type the six digits back is where sign-ups leak most. The browser is already signed into the mailbox, so the new protocol lets it present proof directly; when unsupported, the old flow takes over untouched.

Support Email Verification API: the guide gives no Baseline data, only says to enable an origin trial and mentions Chrome Origin Trial builds; recorded as Limited (Chrome origin trial only)

mwg:verify-email-ownership · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Keep the verification nonce on the server and use it once CorrectionPartialLimited Verify email address ownership · Verifying the wrong identity
Action
Generate a nonce of at least 128 bits on the server for every form render, store it in server-side session state keyed by an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax session cookie; serve the page with Cache-Control: no-store; atomically read and delete the nonce when the POST arrives

Storing the expected nonce directly in a client cookie lets an attacker replay the cookie and token together (quote: "never store the expected nonce value directly inside a client cookie where an attacker could replay both the cookie and token")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — This is a server-side flow design unaffected by browser support; unsupported cases simply run the legacy flow

The token is bound to the nonce; if the nonce also lives on the client, one captured pair works again and again. Keep the nonce on the server and delete it on use, and replay becomes pointless.

Support Same as mwg:verify-email-ownership; recorded as Limited

mwg:verify-email-ownership:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Verify tokens only on the server with established libraries, and check DNS delegation before trusting iss CorrectionPartialLimited Verify email address ownership · Tampering goes undetected
Action
Parse EVT~KB-JWT with SD-JWT/JOSE libraries such as @sd-jwt/core and jose; before trusting iss, check the _email-verification.<domain> DNS TXT delegation and that .well-known/email-verification reports the same issuer; verify the EVT signature and the KB-JWT nonce, audience, freshness, and algorithm allowlist

Verifying tokens in client-side JavaScript can be trivially bypassed or forged and gives the relying party no trust guarantee (quote: "client-side checks can be trivially bypassed or forged and provide zero trust guarantee to the relying party.")

Keeps core behavior — This covers server-side verification and DNS delegation checks without browser feature support issues

The token is a JWT anyone can decode, and glancing at email_verified: true in the front end is easy, but anyone can forge that glance. The real check is on the server: signature, delegation, binding, all of them.

Support Same as mwg:verify-email-ownership; recorded as Limited

mwg:verify-email-ownership:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

When the EVT has no kid, trial each of the provider's keys CorrectionPartialLimited Verify email address ownership · Wrong arguments or formats throw
Action
When jwtVerify throws ERR_JWKS_MULTIPLE_MATCHING_KEYS, iterate the candidate keys from the error with for await and verify against each; during the transition treat Ed25519 and EdDSA as equivalent for the KB-JWT algorithm
Opponent
Providers such as Gmail omit kid from the EVT header, and with multiple keys in the JWKS jose throws outright (quote: "When kid is absent and the JWKS contains multiple keys, jose throws ERR_JWKS_MULTIPLE_MATCHING_KEYS")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — This handles server-side verification failure flows without browser feature support issues

Textbook verification code fails for the biggest email provider, because its tokens don't say which key signed them.

Support Same as mwg:verify-email-ownership; recorded as Limited

mwg:verify-email-ownership:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Scale and fade slides with scroll position using a view() timeline New capabilityPartialNewly Carousel slide effects · Scroll-linked effects rely on JS listeners
Idea · brainstormCover-flow style carousels used to compute each slide in a scroll handler → now photo albums, product carousels, and timelines can scale and fade continuously with scrolling in pure CSS
Action
Give each slide a 0%→50%→100% keyframe animation (e.g. scale 0.5→1→0.5) with animation-timeline: view(inline) (or a named view-timeline) so progress follows the slide through the scrollport; wrap in prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference and @supports, optionally with scroll snap to center
Opponent
The guide only says the native implementation is more performant than a scroll-listener plus Web Animations fallback and that fallbacks can't recreate every effect; it doesn't say when the old approach breaks (quote: "In browsers with built-in support for scroll-driven animations, ALWAYS use the native CSS implementation as those are more performant.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Falling back to scroll listeners plus Web Animations preserves effects while losing native compositor performance
Unlock
Slides can scale or fade continuously along a view() timeline as they pass through the scrollport

Slides that grow in the middle and shrink and fade toward the edges used to mean measuring every slide on every scroll. Now position itself is the animation's timeline.

Support Scroll-driven animations: Newly available (2026-10-27). Supported by: Chrome 115, Edge 115, Firefox 159, Safari 26

mwg:carousel-slide-effects · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Write animation-timeline after the animation shorthand CorrectionPartialNewly Carousel slide effects · Shorthands or linked properties reset settings
Action
Write the animation shorthand first, then animation-timeline and animation-range
Opponent
Writing the shorthand afterwards resets the timeline (quote: "declare animation-timeline and animation-range *after* it to prevent the shorthand from resetting the timeline.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When unsupported, recreate the effect with scroll listeners and Web Animations

The animation shorthand resets every sub-property it covers, animation-timeline included. Reverse the order and the animation goes back to running on time.

Support Same as mwg:carousel-slide-effects; recorded as Newly

mwg:carousel-slide-effects:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

A scroller without focusable content must be focusable itself CorrectionWinN/A Carousel slide effects · Hiding or disabling locks people out

When slides contain no focusable elements, give the scroller tabindex="0" and an accessible name; a <ul> already has the list role, a <div> needs a role that supports naming such as role="region"
Opponent
Not every browser makes a scroll container keyboard-focusable, so keyboard users can't scroll the slides (quote: "because not every browser makes a scroll container keyboard-focusable.")
Fallback
Not needed — Support status is N/A; no fallback needed

Mouse and touch can drag it, but the keyboard can't even get in. A Tab stop and a name fix that.

Support tabindex, role: the guide gives no support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:carousel-slide-effects:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Set color-scheme on a component so its whole subtree uses the other scheme New capabilityPartialNewly Component-specific light/dark themes · Theme colors don't match their context
Idea · brainstormKeeping a component dark used to mean copying a color set while native controls lagged behind → now code blocks, video players, maps, and component previews on a light docs site can each lock their scheme, scrollbars and checkboxes included, with no second stylesheet
Action
With light-dark() color tokens on the page, set color-scheme: dark (or only dark to force it) on self-contained surfaces like code blocks, media players, galleries, and single-scheme embeds; tokens, form controls, and scrollbars in the subtree resolve under that scheme; skip shallow containers that just swap colors, like buttons
Opponent
The guide only lists use cases and says older browsers should switch custom properties on the root with prefers-color-scheme and avoid the media query on individual components; it doesn't say when the old approach breaks (quote: "Avoid using the media query on individual components unless the component requires a very specific type of dark mode customization beyond colors.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Falling back to root media queries and tokens loses per-component native UI theming
Unlock
A single component can override its color scheme so descendant tokens, form controls, and scrollbars switch together

A dark code block on a light page used to need its own set of colors, and its scrollbar stayed light anyway. Now you declare the scheme on that block and the tokens re-resolve themselves.

Support color-scheme: Widely available (2022-02-03); light-dark(): Newly available (2024-05-13), Supported by: Chrome 123, Edge 123, Firefox 120, Safari 17.5

mwg:component-specific-light-dark-theme · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Re-specify inherited color properties on elements that change color-scheme CorrectionPartialNewly Component-specific light/dark themes · Theme colors don't match their context
Action
On the element with the color-scheme override, set color, accent-color, and other inherited color properties again (even to the same token); don't register design tokens as <color> with @property; don't use inherit on color properties of such elements
Opponent
light-dark() resolves at computed-value time, so only one of the two colors is inherited; when a component turns dark, its subtree's accent-color stays the light-scheme value (quote: "any inherited <color> properties set to a light-dark() color will only pass down one of the two colors to their descendants")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When light-dark() is unsupported, switch tokens via media queries and reset component colors

The scheme switched and the background went dark, but the accent color is still the blue meant for a light background. What got inherited was the already-computed color, not the expression that depends on the scheme.

Support light-dark(): Newly

mwg:component-specific-light-dark-theme:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't set color-scheme on elements without a background CorrectionWinWidely Component-specific light/dark themes · Theme colors don't match their context
Action
Override color-scheme only on complex surfaces that have their own background and establish their own visual context
Opponent
Setting color-scheme on an element without a background mixes background and text colors from different schemes, making text unreadable (quote: "Do not set color-scheme on elements without a background, as that risks mixing background and text color pairs from different color-schemes, resulting in unreadable text.")
Fallback
Not needed — color-scheme is already Widely available; no fallback needed

The text follows the element into dark mode and turns light, while the page's light background shows through: white on white.

Support color-scheme: Widely

mwg:component-specific-light-dark-theme:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Safari doesn't pass the embedder's scheme into iframes, so pass it explicitly CorrectionWinWidely Component-specific light/dark themes · Theme colors don't match their context
Action
If you control both sides, pass the parent's scheme to the iframe via a URL parameter (?theme=dark) or postMessage(), and have the iframe set a class or color-scheme on <html> from it; if you only control the embedded page, expose and document an explicit theme parameter in the embed API
Opponent
Safari doesn't render iframes per the embedder's color-scheme, and prefers-color-scheme inside the iframe still follows the system setting (quote: "Safari does not, and resolves prefers-color-scheme to the system setting even inside iframes.")
Fallback
Not needed — color-scheme is already Widely available; no fallback needed

Chrome and Firefox let the iframe follow the outer scheme; Safari doesn't. A bright white widget sits inside a dark page, and the only fix is for both sides to talk through parameters.

Support color-scheme: Widely (see the guide for the iframe behavior difference)

mwg:component-specific-light-dark-theme:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Treat icons as CSS custom properties and let the cascade pick which one shows New capabilityPartialNewly Using and managing icons · Icon styling can't reach the icon
Idea · brainstormIcon color and state used to need filters, file swaps, or class toggles → now a design system can ship its whole icon set as tokens: external links get an external-link icon automatically, expand buttons swap arrows by aria-expanded, and a toolbar resizes and recolors all its icons in one place, with no HTML changes
Action
Each icon is a custom property holding an image (--icon-trash); an element shows one by setting --icon-start/--icon-end; @container style(--icon-start) detects a value and draws it in ::before with mask and currentColor; state changes are just property overrides ([aria-expanded="true"] swaps the icon); size, color, and spacing come from inheritable --icon-style-* set on an ancestor
Opponent
Recoloring icons with <img> plus CSS filters can't reliably apply an arbitrary CSS color, so recoloring is cumbersome and inflexible (quote: "Filters can't reliably apply an arbitrary CSS color value to the image, so recoloring is cumbersome and inflexible.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When style queries are unsupported, attach icons with classes or component selectors
Unlock
Icons can be styled as cascading CSS tokens that switch automatically via selectors or state

An icon used to be another image: filter it or swap the file to change color, hide one and show another to change state. Once an icon is a property, it goes through the cascade like color or font size.

Support Container style queries: Newly available (2026-05-19), Supported by: Chrome 111, Edge 111, Firefox 151, Safari 18; Registered custom properties: Newly available (2024-07-09)

mwg:icons · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Register icon properties as non-inheriting CorrectionPartialNewly Using and managing icons · Inheritance reaches further or less far than expected
Action
@property --icon-start { syntax: "*"; inherits: false; } (same for --icon-end), forwarding the value to the pseudo-element with --icon-start: inherit inside the style query; without @property, reset descendants to initial inside the query
Opponent
If not registered as non-inheriting, an icon set on a button inherits down and every descendant draws one too (quote: "without it, an icon set on a button would inherit into every descendant, and each of them would render the icon too.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When @property is unsupported, reset the icon property to initial on descendants inside the query

Custom properties inherit by default, which is great for tokens and a disaster for this element has an icon: the span inside the button thinks it should draw one too.

Support Registered custom properties: Newly

mwg:icons:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use root-relative URLs or data URIs for icon tokens CorrectionPartialNewly Using and managing icons · Relative URLs resolve against the wrong base
Action
Use root-relative paths (url("/icons/trash.svg")) or data URIs in icon tokens; if relative URLs are unavoidable, register with a syntax starting with <url> and declare the actual URL on :root; with many icons, register them in bulk via CSS.registerProperty
Opponent
A relative URL used through a custom property may resolve against the stylesheet that uses it rather than the one that defines it, pointing to the wrong file when they live in different directories; URLs in a registered property's initial-value only work in Firefox (quote: "If those stylesheets are in different directories, the URL may resolve to the wrong file.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Use root-relative URLs or data URIs so icon tokens resolve reliably everywhere

A token defined in a stylesheet in directory A and used from one in directory B may get resolved with B's path, and the icon breaks.

Support Registered custom properties: Newly

mwg:icons:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Give the icon pseudo-element flex: none so long labels can't squeeze it out CorrectionWinN/A Using and managing icons · Layout unexpectedly overflows or shifts
Action
Set flex: none on the ::before/::after that draws the icon
Opponent
An empty pseudo-element has a zero minimum size, so inside a flex button it's the first thing to shrink when the label is long, possibly to nothing (quote: "inside a flex button it is the first thing to shrink when the label is long, potentially to nothing.")
Fallback
Not needed — Support status is N/A; no fallback needed

After translation into German the button label got longer and the trash icon quietly vanished.

Support flex: the guide gives no support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:icons:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Add forced-color-adjust: none to mask-drawn icons CorrectionWinN/A Using and managing icons · Focus or state indicators disappear
Action
Set forced-color-adjust: none on the pseudo-element that draws the icon and fill with currentColor
Opponent
Forced-colors mode replaces background-color, so an icon drawn with a mask disappears entirely (quote: "In forced-colors mode the browser otherwise replaces background-color, making a masked icon disappear.")
Fallback
Not needed — Support status is N/A; no fallback needed

A mask icon's color is really its background color, and the background color is the first thing forced-colors mode takes away.

Support forced-color-adjust: the guide gives no support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:icons:5 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Inline the SVG the first time, then reuse it with <use href="#id"> CorrectionWinN/A Using and managing icons · Legitimate connections blocked by security rules
Action
Inline the SVG at an icon's first appearance and reference it on the same page with <use href="#id">; keep external sprites (<use href="/icons.svg#id">) for same-origin icons shared across many pages; put viewBox on the <symbol>; namespace symbol ids in inlined sprites
Opponent
External <use> references are same-origin only, and cross-origin sprites fail silently (quote: "External references are same-origin only; cross-origin sprites fail silently.")
Fallback
Not needed — Support status is N/A; no fallback needed

Putting the icon sprite on a CDN seems sensible, until every <use> renders blank with nothing in the console.

Support SVG <use>: the guide gives no support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:icons:6 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Leave custom-property hooks in symbols so <use> icons can be tuned from outside New capabilityPartialLimited Using and managing icons · Icon styling can't reach the icon
Idea · brainstorm<use> icons used to allow little more than recoloring → now one symbol can change stroke width or even its path through CSS variables: play/pause or check/cross share one <use> and change shape with state. Path changes don't work in Safari yet
Action
In symbols you control, add hooks such as fill="var(--icon-accent, currentColor)" and stroke-width="var(--icon-stroke, 2)", even CSS d: var(--icon-path, path(…)) on a path; inline the SVG when you don't control the source
Opponent
Content referenced by <use> is cloned into a shadow tree, so page CSS can't select its elements (quote: "With <use>, the referenced content is cloned into a shadow tree, so page CSS cannot select its elements.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Safari can't change the path with CSS d, but hooks such as fill and stroke width still work
Unlock
Symbols can expose CSS variable hooks so <use> instances customize color, stroke width, or path from outside

<use> is cheap, at the price of page styles not reaching inside. As long as the icon leaves variables in place, you can still tune color and stroke from outside, and in most browsers even the shape.

Support css.properties.d: Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 52, Edge 79, Firefox 97. Unsupported in: Safari

mwg:icons:7 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Patch around two Safari rendering bugs CorrectionPartialNewly Using and managing icons · Browser implementation bugs
Action
Under a Safari-only @supports, apply an empty keyframe animation to ::before/::after inside an @layer; in Safari re-register --icon-start as inheriting and reset descendants to initial inside the style query
Opponent
A WebKit bug can keep icons from appearing until the user interacts; another keeps a direct override of --icon-start on hover from taking effect (quote: "can prevent them from appearing until user interaction")
Fallback
Not stated — The guide provides a Safari bug workaround without covering other unsupported cases

The same icon set works in Chrome, but in Safari it only shows up after a click on the page. The bug is the browser's, but the page has to route around it.

Support Container style queries, registered custom properties: Newly

mwg:icons:8 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Flip the arrow along with the tooltip using anchored container queries New capabilityPartialLimited Position-aware tooltips · Popups detach from their trigger
Idea · brainstormAfter flipping, tooltip arrows used to point the wrong way, so people dropped the arrow or detected it in JS → now help bubbles, onboarding callouts, and chart annotations can keep the arrow pointing at the trigger in pure CSS. Chromium only for now
Action
Build the tooltip with popover and popovertarget (implicit anchor), set position-try-fallbacks: flip-block and container-type: anchored; inside @container anchored(fallback: flip-block) change the direction and position of the inner element's ::before arrow; add an inner wrapper to restyle the box itself
Opponent
The tooltip sits above its anchor with a down arrow; after scrolling it flips below, and the arrow points the wrong way on the wrong side (quote: "If the user scrolls and the tooltip flips to appear *below* the anchor, the arrow is now pointing the wrong way and is on the wrong side of the tooltip.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When anchored queries are unsupported, hide the arrow while tooltips still flip edges
Unlock
CSS can query which anchor fallback actually applied so the arrow direction flips to match

Anchor positioning makes tooltips flip at the edges, but only the browser knew it had flipped, not the arrow. The new query lets styles ask which side am I on now.

Support Anchor position container queries: Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 143, Edge 143. Unsupported in: Firefox, Safari. Popover: Newly (2025-01-27). This guide gives no anchor positioning group status

mwg:position-aware-tooltips · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't let the tooltip cover the control that just got focus CorrectionPartialNewly Position-aware tooltips · Focus or state indicators disappear

When the tooltip may cover the next focused element, reposition it, or dismiss it once it's no longer relevant
Opponent
Keyboard navigation doesn't close a popover=auto tooltip, so it can cover the control that just got focus, failing WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (quote: "Keyboard navigation does not close a popover=auto tooltip, so ensure that tooltips do not obscure interactive elements as they receive focus via keyboard.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Load the polyfill when popover is unsupported to preserve show/hide behavior

Mouse users move away and the tooltip goes; keyboard users carry it with them through every Tab, and the next button sits right under it.

Support Popover: Newly

mwg:position-aware-tooltips:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Idea · brainstormThe initial scroll position used to wait for JS → now inboxes, note lists, and chat logs can open on the main content and reveal search, filters, or load earlier messages only when pulled down. Chromium only for now

This used to be done with scrollIntoView() or a #content-id fragment; the guide only says both have limitations and are tricky, not when they break (quote: "both of which have limitations and are tricky to implement.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When unsupported, use scrollIntoView() to scroll immediately to the main content
Unlock
Scroll containers can start rested on the main content at initial render, keeping top controls tucked away

Pull down to reveal search, common in mobile apps, always needed JS to scroll once after load on the web. The new property lets CSS declare start scrolled here.

Support scroll-initial-target: Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 133, Edge 133. Unsupported in: Firefox, Safari

mwg:pull-to-reveal · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Action
If the target should be the keyboard starting point, call element.focus() yourself
Opponent
The property only moves the visual scroll position, not keyboard focus (quote: "This property only moves the **visual** viewport; it does not move the keyboard focus.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When unsupported, call scrollIntoView() and set keyboard focus manually

The screen starts at the main content, but Tab starts at the hidden search bar, and the first press jumps the view back to the top.

Support Same as mwg:pull-to-reveal; recorded as Limited

mwg:pull-to-reveal:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Every pull-to-reveal action needs a visible button CorrectionWinN/A Pull to reveal · Only reachable by hover

Give every pull-to-reveal action a visible button (or menu item) that does the same thing with one click or Enter, at least 24×24 CSS pixels and named after what it acts on

Not needed — Support status is N/A; no fallback needed

Not needed — Support status is N/A; no fallback needed

Drop a table into a phone or a sidebar and either ten columns squash together or, by column seven, you've forgotten whose row this is. Sticky headers plus cards when narrow keep data and labels connected.

Support position: sticky, container queries: the guide gives no support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:responsive-table · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Support tabindex, role: the guide gives no support data; recorded as N/A

mwg:responsive-table:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Show back to top only after scrolling down, with scroll-state(scrollable: top) New capabilityPartialLimited Scroll-position-aware elements · Scroll-linked effects rely on JS listeners
Idea · brainstormAppear after scrolling floating buttons used to need listeners or sentinels → now back to top on long articles, floating add buttons on long lists, and mini title bars that appear past the intro can decide in pure CSS when to show. Chromium only for now

mwg:scroll-progress-indicator · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't rely on CSS.supports() alone to know if display can transition CorrectionPartialLimited Animate elements to and from the top layer · Feature detection is unreliable
Action
Test whether display transitions actually work with a temporary probe element and also check CSS.supports('overlay', 'auto'), evaluating lazily (the probe needs document.body); if unsupported, take the data-closing fallback and route the cancel event (Esc, closedby) through the same close function
Opponent
Firefox 129+ parses transition-behavior: allow-discrete (CSS.supports() returns true) but doesn't actually transition display, so elements vanish immediately on exit (quote: "Firefox 129+ parses transition-behavior: allow-discrete (CSS.supports('transition-behavior', 'allow-discrete') returns true) without actually transitioning the display property")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Detect via overlay support and a computed-style probe so Firefox/Safari run data-closing to keep exit animations

Detection says supported, and the dialog just disappears. Top-layer elements also need overlay checked; only when both hold can you leave it to CSS.

Support transitionable display, overlay: Limited

mwg:animate-to-from-top-layer:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't put allow-discrete in the transition shorthand CorrectionPartialNewly Animate elements to and from the top layer · Unrecognized syntax invalidates the whole rule
Action
Write a separate transition-behavior: allow-discrete after transition
Opponent
Putting allow-discrete in the transition shorthand makes older browsers ignore the entire transition declaration (quote: "it will make older browsers ignore the entire transition declaration.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Splitting declarations keeps opacity and standard transitions working in older browsers instead of dropping the rule

Just like regular element entry and exit, one new keyword can make older browsers drop the whole transition.

Support transition-behavior: Newly

mwg:animate-to-from-top-layer:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Highlight the snapped carousel item with a scroll-state(snapped) query New capabilityStalemateLimited Carousel snap highlights · Scroll-linked effects rely on JS listeners
Idea · brainstormKnowing which item is centered used to need JS → galleries, product carousels, and timelines can enlarge and color the item that comes to rest in pure CSS. Chromium only for now
Action
Give the scroller scroll-snap-type: x mandatory, make each item container-type: scroll-state, and style the card inside with @container scroll-state(snapped: x), wrapped in prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference
Opponent
The guide only says this avoids relying on IntersectionObserver or scroll listeners, without saying when those approaches go wrong (quote: "without relying on JavaScript intersection observers or scroll event listeners")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Firefox and Safari fall back to unhighlighted basics or an IntersectionObserver script, losing the pure-CSS approach
Unlock
Highlight snapped carousel items in pure CSS with @container scroll-state(snapped) without scroll or observer scripts

Knowing which slide the carousel stopped on used to mean watching a thin strip in the middle with an observer. Snapping is now a queryable state and CSS takes over, but Firefox and Safari can't see it yet.

Support Container scroll-state queries: Limited availability, Supported by: Chrome 144, Edge 144; Unsupported in: Firefox, Safari

mwg:carousel-snap-highlights · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't use the snap highlight as a selection CorrectionPartialLimited Carousel snap highlights · Visual change without semantics or focus
Action
Treat the snap highlight as purely visual; don't let people choose by snapping, don't make the highlight look active or focused, and keep the focus ring distinct from it
Opponent
The snapped state isn't in the accessibility tree; with interactive content inside, moving focus scrolls the container and changes which item is snapped, so the snapped item may not be the focused one (quote: "the snapped item is not exposed to the accessibility tree", "This will likely be a source of confusion for users")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Even when Firefox and Safari use IntersectionObserver highlights, keep snap state distinct from selection and focus rings

"Whatever you scroll to is selected" feels intuitive, but only sighted users know what was chosen, and moving keyboard focus makes the snap jump to another item.

Support Container scroll-state queries: Limited

mwg:carousel-snap-highlights:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Keep non-highlighted items at sufficient contrast CorrectionWinN/A Carousel snap highlights · Hiding or disabling locks people out
Action
Keep items that aren't snapped at sufficient contrast instead of making them greyscale and faded until they snap
Opponent
Non-highlighted content becomes hard to perceive and people can't tell there is more content to navigate to (quote: "don't make the non-highlighted items in a gallery greyscale with a low opacity", "to allow people to understand that there is more content that they can navigate to")
Fallback
Not needed — Support status is N/A; no separate fallback needed

Dimming everything else to spotlight the middle item is the usual move, and it makes the neighbouring content look like it isn't there.

Support Contrast requirement: no support data in the guide, recorded as N/A

mwg:carousel-snap-highlights:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Wait for the new page with blocking="render" and <link rel="expect"> before transitioning New capabilityPartialLimited Consistent cross-document transitions · Wrong lifecycle assumptions
Idea · brainstormShared-element transitions on multi-page sites often landed on a half-rendered page → list-to-article and card-to-detail titles and hero images can reliably fly across without turning the site into an SPA. Firefox falls back to normal navigation
Action
Opt both pages in with @view-transition { navigation: auto; }; mark layout-critical scripts in the new page's <head> with blocking="render", and block painting until above-the-fold elements are parsed with <link rel="expect" href="#main-content" blocking="render">, optionally per viewport via media
Opponent
If the transition starts before the new page's critical resources are ready, it animates to an incomplete or unstyled state; if a morph target hasn't been parsed, the morph degrades to separate fade-out/fade-in (quote: "elements morphing to wrong positions, content reflowing mid-animation, or fallback fonts flashing to web fonts after the transition completes")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Unsupported browsers ignore the rules and perform standard same-origin navigation; supporting ones natively support render blocking
Unlock
Multi-page sites get smooth cross-document transitions without converting to an SPA, waiting for above-the-fold scripts and DOM

A cross-document transition snapshots the old page, navigates, and animates to the new one; the problem is the new-page snapshot being taken too early. Declaring the above-the-fold scripts and elements as render-blocking means it captures the finished page.

Support Cross-document view transitions: Limited availability, Supported by: Chrome 126, Edge 126, Safari 18.2; Unsupported in: Firefox. The guide notes every browser that supports them also supports blocking="render" and <link rel="expect">

mwg:consistent-cross-document-transitions · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

rel="expect" doesn't wait for images: preload and size transition images CorrectionPartialLimited Consistent cross-document transitions · Wrong lifecycle assumptions
Action
Preload morphing images with <link rel="preload" as="image"> (or prerender the destination) and give them width/height or aspect-ratio plus a placeholder background
Opponent
<link rel="expect"> only waits for the element to be parsed, not for image data, so an uncached <img> shows up as an empty box in the new-page snapshot (quote: "an uncached <img> may be captured as an empty rectangle in the new-page snapshot")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers lacking cross-document transitions navigate normally, while preloading and explicit dimensions reserve layout space before decode

The element being there doesn't mean the image has arrived. Even after blocking on the element, the hero can still fly across as a blank box.

Support Cross-document view transitions: Limited

mwg:consistent-cross-document-transitions:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Block only on above-the-fold critical resources; never mark third-party loaders blocking="render" CorrectionPartialLimited Consistent cross-document transitions · Over-applied optimizations backfire
Action
Use blocking="render" and rel="expect" only for resources and elements that affect the first viewport; leave analytics, ads, and tag managers out; keep render-blocking scripts small and fast
Opponent
Blocking too much delays the transition; if render blocking exceeds about 4 seconds the browser skips the transition entirely and viewTransition.ready rejects with InvalidStateError, and third-party latency counts toward that timeout (quote: "Their network latency counts toward the transition timeout")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When exceeding timeout or unsupported, transitions skip cleanly and the page still renders without blocking navigation

To make the transition steadier you block on more and more; block on one slow third-party script and the transition simply doesn't happen.

Support Cross-document view transitions: Limited

mwg:consistent-cross-document-transitions:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

No duplicate view-transition-name on a page CorrectionPartialLimited Consistent cross-document transitions · Transitions skipped or broken
Action
Give each view-transition-name to only one element per page
Opponent
Duplicate names make the whole transition be skipped (quote: "Duplicate names cause the entire transition to be skipped.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Duplicate names or lack of support only skip the transition animation while page navigation keeps working

Giving every card in a list the same name is easy to do, and the result isn't one card without animation but the whole navigation without one.

Support Cross-document view transitions: Limited

mwg:consistent-cross-document-transitions:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Remove names assigned in pagereveal once the transition finishes CorrectionPartialLimited Consistent cross-document transitions · Wrong lifecycle assumptions
Action
Assign view-transition-name in pagereveal based on where the user came from, clear it after viewTransition.finished, and register the listener early from a blocking="render" script
Opponent
Temporary names left in place interfere with later navigations and keep the page out of the bfcache; a listener registered too late (for example in a deferred script) misses the event (quote: "Stale names interfere with subsequent navigations and prevent the page from entering the bfcache.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers lacking cross-document transitions skip pagereveal and navigate normally; clearing temp names preserves bfcache

A heading gets a temporary name so the morph only happens when coming from the list; forget to take it back and both the return transition and the back/forward cache suffer.

Support Cross-document view transitions: Limited

mwg:consistent-cross-document-transitions:5 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Give multi-page sites page transitions with @view-transition New capabilityPartialLimited Cross-document transitions · Size changes jump instead of animating
Idea · brainstormAnimated page changes used to require an SPA → statically generated sites (docs, portfolios, journals) get transitions from two lines of CSS. Firefox falls back to normal navigation
Action
In a stylesheet shared by both pages, write @view-transition { navigation: auto; } inside prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference, then customize slide-out/slide-in with ::view-transition-old(root) / ::view-transition-new(root)
Opponent
The guide only says it creates smooth, app-like transitions between pages, without saying when a normal navigation goes wrong (quote: "create smooth, app-like transitions between different pages of a Multi-Page Application (MPA)")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers lacking cross-document transitions fall back to standard instant page loads with core navigation intact
Unlock
Plain multi-page sites gain customizable, app-like page transitions with CSS alone instead of rewriting as an SPA

Page changes on multi-page sites have always been a full-page flash. Now one declaration on each page gives a transition, and unsupported browsers navigate as usual with no fallback to write.

Support View transitions: Newly (2025-10-14); Cross-document view transitions: Limited availability, Supported by: Chrome 126, Edge 126, Safari 18.2; Unsupported in: Firefox

mwg:cross-document-transitions · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Use transition types so "back" and "forward" move in opposite directions New capabilityPartialLimited Cross-document transitions · Size changes jump instead of animating
Idea · brainstormTransitions on multi-page sites couldn't tell direction → step-by-step tutorials, previous/next in galleries, and article series can each slide the right way. Firefox falls back to normal navigation
Action
When a page always uses one direction, write types: previous in @view-transition; when it depends on the origin, compute a type from navigation.activation in pagereveal and call e.viewTransition.types.add(), then style each with :active-view-transition-type()
Opponent
With one effect for every navigation, going back to the home page slides in from the right just like going forward, which makes no spatial sense (quote: "When navigating back to the home page, it wouldn't make sense to have the same effect.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Use alternate logic or a default transition type when Navigation API is missing, or fall back to instant loads if unsupported
Unlock
Multi-page sites can switch slide directions dynamically based on forward/back navigation history and source page

As soon as a slide transition works you notice going back also "slides forward". Types let the same set of pages choose an animation by how they relate.

Support Cross-document view transitions: Limited; Navigation API: Newly (2026-01-13)

mwg:cross-document-transitions:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Declare what a button does to which element with command="--custom" New capabilityPartialNewly Custom button actions · Wiring JS to every button
Idea · brainstormA set of controls used to need JS wired to each button → player, canvas editor, and kanban card actions can be written in HTML as --play, --zoom-in, --archive, and server-rendered pages ship working buttons
Action
Give buttons commandfor="target-id" and a custom command starting with -- such as command="--spin"; listen for command on the target, look up event.command in a registry, and use event.source to update the button's aria-pressed / aria-expanded
Opponent
The guide only says it reduces manual event listeners and decouples UI from implementation, without saying when hand-wired listeners go wrong (quote: "This approach reduces the need for manual event listeners and decouples the UI from implementation details.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When unsupported, conditionally load invokers-polyfill or use click delegation so button actions keep working
Unlock
Declarative HTML button attributes trigger custom actions on targets, cutting boilerplate listeners and decoupling UI from logic

Each button used to get its own addEventListener and find its target, so renaming an id meant editing JS. Now buttons just declare "to whom, what", and behaviour lives in one command table on the target.

Support Invoker commands: Newly (2025-12-12), Supported by: Chrome 135, Edge 135, Firefox 144, Safari 26.2

mwg:custom-button-actions · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

command doesn't bubble: attach the listener to the target CorrectionPartialNewly Custom button actions · Non-bubbling events never arrive
Action
Attach the command listener directly to the target; when targets vary, listen on an ancestor with { capture: true }; when the target may be in a shadow root, use event.composedPath()[0]
Opponent
The command event doesn't bubble, so a delegated listener on an ancestor never receives it (quote: "The command event does not bubble.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Listen with { capture: true } on ancestors for multiple targets; polyfill or click delegation still fires in unsupported browsers

Anyone used to delegating events on document writes their first command handler and finds nothing happens.

Support Invoker commands: Newly

mwg:custom-button-actions:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Open and close dialogs from HTML with command="show-modal" and toggle-popover New capabilityPartialNewly Declarative dialog and popover control · Wiring JS to every button
Idea · brainstormModal dialogs always needed JS to open → plain HTML pages (docs, form confirmations, image lightboxes) get dialogs with native focus handling that still open if scripts break
Action
<button commandfor="id" command="show-modal"> opens a modal <dialog> and command="close" closes it; popovers use toggle-popover, or separate show-popover / hide-popover
Opponent
The guide only says it removes brittle boilerplate and makes interactions work as soon as HTML is parsed, without saying when hand-written listeners go wrong (quote: "removes brittle boilerplate code, ensures interactions are functional immediately upon HTML parsing")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Older browsers conditionally load invokers and popover polyfills so toggling dialogs and popovers keeps working
Unlock
Open and close dialogs and popovers declaratively from HTML upon parse with built-in focus management and ARIA bindings

Opening a confirm dialog used to take at least a snippet of showModal() JS. Now the button points straight at the dialog and it opens and closes before any script runs.

Support Invoker commands: Newly (2025-12-12); Popover: Newly (2025-01-27)

mwg:declarative-dialog-popover-control · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Don't put both popovertarget and commandfor on one button CorrectionPartialNewly Declarative dialog and popover control · Two mechanisms acting twice
Action
Use either popovertarget or commandfor to control a given popover, not both
Opponent
Using both toggles the popover twice and breaks it (quote: "This will double-toggle it, breaking functionality.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Using only one attribute per popover alongside polyfill fallbacks keeps toggling reliable without double-toggles

Both declarative toggles do the same job; stack them and it opens and immediately closes.

Support Invoker commands: Newly; Popover: Newly

mwg:declarative-dialog-popover-control:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

When closing a popover from inside it, return focus to the trigger CorrectionPartialNewly Declarative dialog and popover control · Hiding or disabling locks people out
Action
When a hide-popover button inside the popover closes it, add script that moves focus back to the button that opened it
Opponent
The close button is hidden along with the popover and focus is lost (quote: "will result in a loss of focus as the button will be hidden and won't retain focus")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Pairing polyfills with a focus-return script preserves keyboard navigation in both native and polyfilled browsers

The moment you press "Close", that button disappears too, and keyboard users are dropped back at the top of the page.

Support Invoker commands: Newly; Popover: Newly

mwg:declarative-dialog-popover-control:3 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

With the popover polyfill, don't set the popover property and wrap :popover-open in :is() CorrectionPartialNewly Declarative dialog and popover control · Unrecognized syntax invalidates the whole rule
Action
Before the polyfill loads, use setAttribute() / removeAttribute() for popover; write styles as [popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open); load the polyfill only when HTMLElement.prototype lacks popover
Opponent
Setting the IDL property before the polyfill loads means the element is never picked up and the polyfill's accessor is shadowed forever; a bare :popover-open makes browsers that don't know it drop the whole rule (quote: "otherwise browsers that lack :popover-open discard the entire rule")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Conditional polyfill loading, setAttribute, and :is() selectors let older browsers open and style popovers properly

The polyfill can't create a real pseudo-class or intercept a property set too early; write it the native way and in older browsers the popover won't open or won't be styled.

Support Popover: Newly

mwg:declarative-dialog-popover-control:4 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Give SPA navigation forward/back direction with typed view transitions New capabilityPartialNewly Directional navigation transitions · Size changes jump instead of animating
Idea · brainstormDirection used to need an animation library plus state management → multi-step forms, slideshows (up/down), and product browsing (left/right) can pick the slide direction with one types argument
Action
Pass forward / backward to document.startViewTransition({ update, types: [direction] }), and in CSS apply matching transform slides with html:active-view-transition-type(forward)::view-transition-old(root), using non-linear easing on ::view-transition-group(root)
Opponent
SPA view changes just replace the content with no transition (quote: "By default, the content is simply replaced, without any transitions.")
Fallback
Loses the main benefit — Fall back to updating the DOM immediately, still with no directional transition
Unlock
SPAs can animate directional forward/back slide transitions with one type parameter without external animation libraries

An SPA "next page" just swaps the content, and users can't feel where they're going. Passing direction as a transition type lets one set of CSS tell forward from back.

Support View transitions: Newly (2025-10-14); Active view transition: Newly (2026-01-13)

mwg:directional-navigation-transitions · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Still update the DOM when startViewTransition is missing CorrectionPartialNewly Directional navigation transitions · No guard for unsupported browsers
Action
Have the navigate function check document.startViewTransition and call updateDOM() directly when it doesn't exist
Opponent
In unsupported browsers document.startViewTransition is undefined; calling it without detection means the view never updates (quote: "In unsupported browsers, document.startViewTransition will be undefined.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Bypassing transitions when feature detection fails ensures older browsers still update the DOM instead of hanging navigation

The transition is a bonus; the navigation isn't. Wrap the transition in detection so only the animation can fail.

Support View transitions: Newly

mwg:directional-navigation-transitions:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Move the real DOM nodes instead of faking order with CSS New capabilityPartialLimited Reordering with drag and drop · Visual order drifts from DOM order
Idea · brainstormA playing video, a live iframe widget or a half-filled form can be moved elsewhere without resetting. Previously every move reloaded it, which made a rearrangeable live dashboard painful.
Action
On drop, move the existing node once with container.moveBefore(item, ref) so visual, keyboard and reading order stay aligned
Opponent
Changing on-screen order with CSS order or flex-direction: *-reverse leaves DOM order unchanged, so Tab and screen readers follow the old order (quote: "Reorder the real children in the DOM (not via CSS order or flex-direction: *-reverse) so visual, keyboard, and reading order stay aligned.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers lacking moveBefore() fall back to before()/append(), keeping DOM order right while losing pointer capture, focus, and media/input state
Unlock
Atomic node moves via moveBefore() preserve focus, input values, scroll positions, media playback, custom element state, and pointer capture

The cheapest drag-to-reorder is changing order: it looks right, but keyboard users jump through the old order. The guide moves the real node once on release and uses moveBefore() to keep focus and iframe state. When visual and DOM order truly cannot match in a complex layout, reading-flow is the tool, but only Chrome/Edge support it.

Support moveBefore(): Limited (Chrome 133, Edge 133, Firefox 144; not Safari); reading-flow: Limited (Chrome/Edge 137; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:drag-and-drop · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Show a drop marker while dragging; move only on release CorrectionWinWidely Reordering with drag and drop · Jitter during interaction
Action
Keep the source item in its slot during the drag, draw a drop marker with ::before/::after, and move on pointerup
Opponent
Reordering live while dragging makes siblings shift and the list jitter (quote: "Don't reorder while the pointer moves: shifting siblings feel jittery.")
Fallback
Not needed — Pointer events and pseudo-element drop markers are both Widely available; no fallback needed

Many drag implementations reorder on pointermove, so the whole list jumps every time the pointer passes an item. The guide shows only a drop line during the drag, moves once on release, and animates every move so items travel instead of jumping.

Support Pointer events: Widely

mwg:drag-and-drop:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Remember the grab offset and clamp to the viewport so dragged elements don't jump or get lost CorrectionWinN/A Build a draggable element · Jitter during interaction
Action
Use position: fixed for the floating panel; start only on the primary button, record the pointer offset on pointerdown, use setPointerCapture() so the drag continues after the pointer leaves the handle; route pointer and arrow-key moves through one clamping helper and re-clamp when the viewport or element resizes
Opponent
Without the offset the element jumps when grabbed away from its corner; without clamping it can be dragged out of view and can't be retrieved (quote: "so the element does not jump when grabbed away from its corner", "so the element stays reachable")
Fallback
Not needed — Pointer events and clamping use existing capabilities; without JS the element remains visible and usable in its default position

The first flaw in a drag is usually "it jumps when grabbed", the second "once it's off-screen you can't get it back". Offset and clamping live in one helper that the keyboard path shares.

Support Pointer events / pointer capture: no support data in the guide, recorded as N/A

mwg:drag · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Apply drag styles to the handle, not the whole element CorrectionPartialLimited Build a draggable element · Hand-built controls lose native behavior
Action
Put cursor: grab, touch-action: none, -webkit-user-select: none, and user-select: none only on a dedicated drag handle, a focusable <button> whose name mentions the arrow keys
Opponent
On the whole draggable element, text inside can't be selected and touch gestures lose their usual behavior; Safari doesn't support unprefixed user-select (quote: "so text outside it remains selectable and touch gestures retain their usual behavior")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Adding -webkit-user-select: none lets Safari suppress text selection properly while dragging the handle

Support user-select: Limited availability, Supported by: Chrome 54, Edge 79, Firefox 69; Unsupported in: Safari

mwg:drag:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Stagger list items into view with sibling-index() New capabilityPartialNewly Creating a stagger animation · JS patches in styling state
Idea · brainstormStaggered entrances needed JS to set each delay → search results, notification lists, and dashboard cards can appear one after another in pure CSS and stay in step when the count changes

animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * var(--stagger-time)) delays each item by its position; disable under reduced motion; for older browsers, use a JS-set --sibling-index as the base declaration and wrap the sibling-index() rule in an @supports test that uses a literal time value
Opponent
The guide only describes the stagger effect, without saying when the old approaches (per-item :nth-child or JS delays) go wrong (quote: "multiple ordered elements animate sequentially with a slight delay between each, rather than all animating at once")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — When unsupported, JS writes --sibling-index and sibling-index() sits inside @supports, so older browsers still stagger entry animations
Unlock
Pure CSS staggers list or menu entry animations sequentially and recalculates delays automatically as item counts change

Stagger delays used to come from JS or a long list of nth-child rules. Now CSS knows "which one am I", and adding or removing items needs no recalculation.

Support sibling-count() and sibling-index(): Newly (2026-08-18), Supported by: Chrome 138, Edge 138, Firefox 154, Safari 26.2

mwg:dynamic-sibling-animations · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Sort by moving existing nodes, not rebuilding with innerHTML New capabilityPartialLimited User-triggered dynamic sorting · Rebuilding the DOM loses state
Idea · brainstormAfter sorting or filtering, the list animates items to their new places with a view transition while scroll, focus and playback inside each item survive. Suits lists of heavy items (embedded previews, video cards).
Action
When the user changes sort order, move the existing nodes into the new order with moveBefore(), optionally wrapped in a view transition
Opponent
Creating new nodes with innerHTML or a full re-render loses focus, scroll position inside items and image state, and breaks view transitions (quote: "Recreating nodes with innerHTML or a re-render that replaces them discards focus, scroll position inside items, and image state, and it breaks view transitions, which match old and new elements by identity.")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Safari lacks moveBefore() and falls back to append(), preserving DOM order while resetting focus and internal item state
Unlock
Reorder existing DOM items without rebuilding nodes, preserving inner focus, iframes, and animations alongside view transitions

Redrawing the whole list after sorting is the usual approach, and the cost is that the button the user just clicked loses focus and a half-scrolled card jumps to the top. The guide turns sorting into "moving house" rather than "rebuilding", with animation as an optional enhancement.

Support moveBefore(): Limited (not Safari); View transitions: Newly (2025-10-14)

mwg:dynamic-sort · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Announce the sort result once CorrectionWinWidely User-triggered dynamic sorting · Over-announcing

Opponent
Putting aria-live on the list makes every moved item get announced (quote: "DO NOT put aria-live on the list, which would announce every moved item.")

A reorder moves many nodes, but the user did one thing. With aria-live on the list, screen readers treat every node move as an update. A single status region announcing once is enough.

Support ARIA live regions: Widely

mwg:dynamic-sort:2 · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0

Define a whole group's transition once with view-transition-class New capabilityPartialNewly Smoothly rearrange cards, lists, and groups of elements on add, remove, or reorder · Style logic duplicated everywhere
Idea · brainstormAnimating list adds, removes, and reorders needed a FLIP library → to-do lists, shopping carts, and kanban columns can slide new items in, slide removed ones out, and close the gaps with one set of CSS

The guide only says that without a class you repeat the transition logic for every name, without saying when the repetition causes an observable problem (quote: "define that logic once in CSS rather than repeating it for every unique view-transition-name")
Fallback
Keeps core behavior — Browsers lacking view-transition-class ignore the styling rule, while browsers lacking view transitions update the DOM directly

A list with dozens of items needs a name per item to be tracked, but the animation should be written once. The class separates "which is which" from "how it moves".

mwg:group-element-transitions · Upstream guide · Line file · v1.0.0
